Engagements in the vicinity Of Buis-
sierre and Thuin constituted the most de-
termined resistance offered by the allies
After two days continuous artillery duel,
which swept the surrounding country and
demolished almost every structure, the
entire right wing Of the allies withdrew
far to the southwark. This gave the Ger
mans an opportunity to sweep through
Beaumont and approach Maubeuge from
the south.


Meanwhile the other corps had ap-
preached Maubeuge from the north, en-
tireiy Investing the fortress. The English
and French were August q driven across
the Sambre river, where on the south
bank of the river in thirty-mile front
fighting continued for three days.


The correspondent first saw actual fir
ing in the direction Of Maubeuge August
26, when white puffs of the German
shrapnel clouded the horizon, but the for
ward movement of the German columns
was SO fast that when the correspondent
reached the scene of the recent engage
ment the firing line had advanced fully
ten miles southwark An extensive
trench system. laid out by the French in
fantry, marked the French retreat


The German wounded, in all cases,
were Immediately cared for and the dead
buried as fast as the army continued on
the march, while the French dead were
left unburied and the wounded, In some
cases, remained on the battlefield for
three days before receiving attention.

NEW YORK. March 14.-Lieuten-
ant Charles Pendleton is in a serious
condition and Colonel Babbitt and a
crew of eighteen men are recovering
from the shock received when a new
twelve-inch gun being tested at the
proving grounds at Sandy Hook burst
and scattered pieces of the 1000 pound
breech block all over the reservation.


The huge iron fragments smashed
through the concrete wall where the
men had taken cover back of the gun.
The wooden platform on which they
were standing was shattered, and
several of the men were thrown down.
Lieutenant Pendleton, however, was
the only man injured.


Precautions are always taken at the
first firing of new gun, and always
the men get under cover until one
shot has been fired, so all possibility
of danger seemed to have been met


When the gun was fired there was a
roar, and the entire breech block,
shattered into big pieces, came flying
directly backward

Washingtons citizen soldiery is now on
the way to its camp grounds at Virginia
Beach, Va, aboard the Dreamland. The
big vessel. bearing the LIST and I'd Regi-
ments Of Infantry. the Signal Corps. Field
Hospital and LIST Separate Battalion. left
her dock shortly after ! o'clock this
morning.


After their first taste of real army life
that of sleeping in the open fields in low
shelter tents and cooking their own
breakfasts this morning-the local soldier
boys rolled up their tents. slung them
over their shoulders and started for the
steamer.


When the bugler sounded reveille about
dawn this morning many Of the soldier
boys used to sleeping until mother calls
four or five times turned over and gave
a sleepy grunt. but they got up, for they
knew that the bugle sound was law and
they must arise. And there was no table
with linen covering, with servants to
serve breakfast. These soldiers just arose.
folded their beds, opened their knapsacks,
took out their breakfasts and cooked
them over the big wood fires which the
cook had provided. That's all the cook
has to do when the boys sleep in shelter
tents while en- route. He lights the fires
and the boys do their own cooking. But
then he has the harder job of getting
up some minutes earlier to get the fire
started.


And judging from the expressions on
the boys faces, those breakfasts tasted
good, even If they did cook them. The
pans in which they cooked and from
which they ate were cleaned and slowed
away in the knapsacks and everything
was ready for the start for the boat.

ing of discomfort Finally the general

erty anyway was carried to its logical

Police Sergeant Brown, prowling
along Forsyth street shortly before
daybreak Friday stopped suddenly
and shifted. He walked slowly down
the street. holding his head high and
smelling vigorously. After going
half block. he bumped into Po-

his head in the air, and was searching
eagerly with his smelling apparatus.

searched every alley and looked into
every house in radius of two blocks.
and finally, having wandered to
Broad and Alabama streets, they
looked into the window Of Keeney's
saloon at No. IL South Broad street,

through the intercession of Luis Cab
rera and ]. II. Belt, Secretary Sllliman

ball.

THE new high bust corset, which
! comes four inches above the waist
line and is Just high enough to form
support for the base of the bust. is the
corset to be worn with the new style
bodices The top is just full enough for
the flesh to rest easily inside the corset.
Then there will be no pushing up of the
bust, no COMPRISING of the diaphragm.


There is a great difference between the
old and the new style of high-bust cor
sets To preserve the large waist which
is still fashionable, these new corsets
are made with full back. Some also
have small gussets underneath each shoul-
der blade, while others have sufficient
fulness to form ripple at the top. The
skirt of these corsets is long over the
thighs in the back, with a slightly short
ened line in front, the fiat back and the
large waist with a slight curve at the
side-fronts. The materials are soft and
pliable and the boning light.


Accentuates Curves.


The reason for the change of cut of
corsets is the semi-fitting character OF
the fashionable dresses and waists. which
makes necessary corsets which hold the
bust in slightly higher position. These
dresses are not tight. but they are semi
fitted, with a dart over the Dust 10 az
centuate the curve. whether the garment
fits snugly or otherwise.


These bodices are In several styles.
Some are buttoned straight in front, with
plain front sections which are darted
and have under-arm cores. Others are
in surplice effects, the crossover pieces
being drawn tightly over the bust. High
girdles are also In fashion, which are OF
the same height all around, reaching
point even with the base Of the bust
Sometimes the girdle is drawn in at the
front Again it may have buttons from
the top of the lower edge. over these
fitted girdles the bust would fall loosely
If it were not supported by the corset.


There are also low-bust corsets for
the slender and compact figures. which
will wear garments suitable for them.
There are also models designed espe-
cially for dancing, which have a shorter
skirt in front and elastic inserts in the
back The tops of these are low, and
there is an elastic band around the top
edge from side to side. For the school
girl there are low and medium-sized cor
set waists with long corset skirts and
front steel fastening. These corset waists
SO closely resemble the regular coret that
young girls feel quite satisfied with them.

Petrograd, Oct. 22.-The Russians

1t was operating toward Warsaw be-

The Grand Duke Nicholas does not

Got Near TO Warsaw.

Skernievice, within q few miles of

The 18th and 18th German Army

ward alone the whole line, some 26O

trian forces from the San River. Here

have only to deal with Austrian corps

the Galician battles. The broken rem
nants of these conquered forces have
been pulled together into some sort Of
formation and put under German COM
mand, but their fighting value has not
in any way been increased by this last
unpalatable measure.


OF the details of the fighting 1t Is
not expected that much will be heard
until the entire operation is COM

hard upon the German retreat, which is
over abominable sloughs of roads
fringed by bog land and marshy forest.
Prisoners and trophies of success are

twelve hundred Princeton undergradu-
ates were on hand this afternoon TO
cheer the Princeton eleven IN Its fnal


practice for to-morrow's game with
Dartmouth. The students marched to
the new Palmer Stadium and kept up a
constant din of cheers and songs as
long as Captain BALM and his men
were at work.


The weird echoes from the empty
west side of the horseshoe caused
much merriment. The day was not
one of absolute rest for the Tiger
players. as the coaches are looking
ahead to the big games to follow, and
cannot train merely for the contest
with Dartmouth. They expect, how
ever, that the Green team will proba-
bly, give the Tigeres as much trouble
as any team on the schedule.

quarters of an hour was followed by
light scrimmage with the scrub, last
ing for about ten minutes. The punt
crs and drop kickers were limbered
up and the ends sent down 10 cover
kicks and forward passes. Actual in
reference was formed, but no tackling
was permitted.


Ames ran the team most of the time,
Eberstadt going in at quarter for only
a short part of the signal drill. Havi-
land occupied centre for the entire
afternoon. but it was explained that
Gennert was detained by some neces-
cary laboratory work and that his abb
sence from the lineup to-day would
not exclude him from the game to-
morrow.

Roland will not get into the tussle
with Dartmouth, for he was not used
even on the second team to-day. The
coaches say he is in poor condition
and may not get back TO form before
the Harvard game.

championship team, reached here to-
day from Chicago and looked the team
over. He will take the line men in
hand on Monday and stay with them
for three weeks. "Now we'll see some
real pep" was the general comment of
the undergraduates when they saw
Hart on the field. His fighting spirit
will undoubtedly be felt tomorrow.


Penheld intimated after the practice
this afternoon that probably three
pairs of ends would be used to-mor-
row. Strong reserves also are ready
for the backfcld.

London, Oct 15.-"The Daily Chroni-

following under date OF yesterday;


"when l left Ostond to-day the Ger

passed forward very rapidly from
Bruges. They were still engaged with
the rear guard of the defending force.
Il perhaps is little TO be wondered at
that tho Belgians after all these long
months Of fighting were dispirited, war
worn and somewhat disorganized.
These brave little soldiers have fought
as no other army ever fought before.
They have sacrificed everything for
their country. For two days there has
been severe fighting on the line from
Client to Bruges and thence toward
0stend.


CAS- one who had been with the Bel
eian soldiers throughout the war, and
who has had occasion 10 admire their
pluck and courage and their heroic
self-sacrifce, il was with deep feelings
of pity that | saw the disintegrated sec
lions Of the army arrive in Ostend
from all parts of the theatre of war.
They had fought and bled, but their
spirits still were unbroken. Here were
men in tattered clothes, some wounded,
the majority starving, having been
without food for days, but there was no
complaining, and after having talked
with many of the officers and men l
came away impressed with the convlc-

important news today would instantly get
out an extra edition, for the whole country
was waiting patiently for word that peace
had been concluded.

What modern medical science can accomplish

will spread from city TO city and State to

GENEVA, November 1s.-The cargo
boats that formerly carried coal and
cereals on the Rhine have been trans
ferred into ambulances. and are con-
veying wounded soldiers from Colmar
to Cologne.


The German wounded generally are
well cared for in the hospitals along
the Rhine. but their numbers have in
creased to such an extent since the mid
die of October that there have not been
enough doctors to give them prompt
attention. and many slightly wounded
have died on this account. So over
worked are the surgeons that they
often fall asleep while on duty.


A story comes from Colmar to the
effect that a well known surgeon. after
having worked for a fortnight with
very little rest. fell asleep over an i'm
portant operation. Pressing calls have
been made upon the doctors In Ger
many, including the most aged. to
remedy the difficulty.

London, June 26.-There were many
novel features about the inverted
Cinderella ball for the blind, which
started at the Savoy Hotel at mid
night and which was still whirling
merrily at a. m. The tickets cost
s26 each, but, as the attendance was
limited to 1900, $50 was readily paid
for a single ticket yesterday.


The price, however, was not the
most striking feature of this wonder
full ball. which owed its origin and
success to c. Arthur Pearson, whose
campaign for the National Institute
for the Blind. has been so consistently
successful. Some exceptional features
were that the ball started at midnight
with a supper and ended long after
breakfast, which was served at a.
m. There were no tangoes and no
maXiXes.

HERE is another arithmetical puzzle that
it might amuse someone to figger out. !"


A poor woman carrying basket of apples
was met by three boys, the first of whom
bought half of what she had and then gave
her back ten; the second boy bought a third
Of what remained, and gave her back two;
and the third bought half of what she now
had left, and returned her one, after which
she found that she had twelve apples re
naming. What number had she at first?


The answer is simple enough: From the
twelve apples remaining, deduct one, and
eleven is the number she sold the last boy,
which was half of all she had; her number at
that time, therefore, was twenty two From
twenty-five deduct two, and the remaining
twenty was two-thirds of her prior stock,
which was therefore thirty. From thirty de-
duct ten, and the remainder of twenty is
half of her original stock; consequently she
had at first forty apples. See9

Block Island, r. l., Aug. S.-The
picturesque town Of New Shoreham,
better known to the many summer Wis
itors as Block Island, has again opened
its doors to weary sojourners from
cities all over the country. From
North and South, and even the Far
West, they come by every boat, some to
ENJOY the whole season and others to
spend their all too short vacation
where they know a good time awaits
them. Perhaps they remember the
bathing, the fishing trips, the many
pleasant walks along the country roads
and the beaches and numerous jolly
evenings spent dancing in one OF the
many hotel bathrooms. 1t may be one
thing or another, but there is always
that mystic something" that draws
one back to Block Island every year.


During July and August the Montauk
Steamboat Company sends boat five
times q week to the island, and the sail
is really part of the pleasure of the
trip.


The bathing conditions this year, rs
always, are ideal, and Crescent Beach,


just south of Clay Head, is thronged
with bsthers morning and afternoon.
Here old and young spend many pleas
ant hours, and children may frolic and
play about in the water without fear
The beach, having a natural curve, is
sandy and smooth and without under
tow Experts say that owing to the
changing northern current of the Gulf
Stream the temperature of the water is
much warmer this year than other sea-
sons. This TENDS to make the bathing
healthful and refreshing


Fishing, though it has always been
the favorite sport with many of the
enthusiasts of the rod and reel, is UNI
usually popular this year. Other sum-
mers it has been the fad to make up
parties and go out with one of the
many captains of the fishing feet to
troll for bluefish, or to be an interested
onlooker to the fight for the mighty
swordfsh. This year as soon as it be-
came known that the tuna could be
caught off the Block Island shores the
sportsmen began to appear in large
numbers. The tuna has always been
found along the Pacific Coast and Of
late in the Florida waters. Here the
sport and fishing clubs accept only
those as members who have caught a
tuna of a certain weight. The mighty
fish are running in great numbers, and,
though they are being caught each
trip, the fisherman often fights hours
for a single tuna.


Block Island has two hundred fresh
water ponds, none of which has either
visible inlet or outlet. These ponds
are filled with fresh water fish, and
the ardent fisherman may hire a row.
boat and fish by the hour for pickerel,
black bass, perch and trout. The
ponds, both large and small, are now
beautiful with water lilies, both white
and golden, and the little island boys
are doing a rousing business selling
these lilies to the visitors at the MANY
hotels.


Perhaps the most popular of all the
walks is along the cliffs to the South
Light. The Mohegan Bluffs rise 200
feet above the sea level and far down
telow us the mighty surf beats cease
lessly. After a good "southeaster" the
waves are wonderful and you feel re-
paid a hundred times for the walk
over to see them. On leaving the Light
one may walk home along the beach
way into the village again. About half
a mile from the town you come to
Pebbly Beach. This is one mass of
rocks large and small, and is noted for
it's garnets, which may be found by
careful searching. Many very fine
specimens have been found and when
polished are beautiful.


Any one who has visited any of the
quaint little fishing ports along the
New England coast knows the charm
of the little village with its narrow
winding streets and dozens of little
shops. Perhaps one of the most nota-
BILE reminders of bygone days is the
little horsecar line which runs from
the Old Harbor past the bathing beach
to the New Harbor, and for five cent
fare you may ride part way to the ball
game and have all your breath saved to
cheer for your favorite team.


The many hotels both large and
small were never so we'll equipped as
now 10 entertain the visitors arriving on
every boat. There are spacious verandas
with the inviting row of rocking chairs,
the cool dining rooms, with the flower
decorated tables, the CHEEKY and sunny
sleeping rooms. and the attractive ball
room, where the music invites one TO
dance away the summer evenings.


The drives about the island are many
and varied, each in its way more in
teresting than the other. So much
is to be seen along the shores that it
would take hours TO tell. This year
whales have been seen along the island
coast in large numbers, and this lis 4
bit unusual. The trial races for the
Americas Cup have been attended by
great excitement on the various hotel
piazzas. for the Old Harbor Break
water was chosen as one point for the
triangular race, and it brought the
beautiful yachts very near to Crescent
Reach.


The midsummer season is in full
swing and all the houses, large and
small, are crowded to their utmost.
The week has been one round of gayety
and fun for all, and if indications are
correct the season of 1914 will be
record breaker.

NEW YORK, Sept 25.-when the Royal
Mall steam packet Magdalena, which ar
rived here from Southampton, left the
latter place a few days ago there were
277 miles of ships moored in the Solent,
stretching from north of Netley to Ports
mouth, according to C. w. Harty, purser
of the Magdalena.


The purser said soldiers, sailors army
nurses and British scouts were permitted
TO ride free in the trains in English cities.
and that the scouts were doing useful
work carrying dispatches. Only three
trains were run daily between Southamp-
ton and London, and passengers were not
permitted on the platforms until the train
came in. Persons in automobiles were
stopped by the military and the machines
seized for war purposes.


Five of the big royal mail liners in the
Brazil trade, the Amazon, Arlanza, Avon
Aragon and Asturas, have been comman-
deered by the Government, two for hos
pital purposes and three for transport
work, Harty said.

fine or imprisonment for a year or both.

ANTWERP. via London. October 90
Upon his arrival in Antwerp the cor
respondent of the Associated Press
found the city guarded by bluejackets
and marine infantrymen from the Ger
man stations at Kiel, Cuxhaven and
Wilhelmshaven. They were smelling
the salt water again after a campaign
of more than a month through Belgium
and awaiting further orders.


Detachments of sailors among them,
recruited from the German merchant
marine. were armed only with cutlasses
behind the army, taking no part in the
fighting, and evidently are destined for
sea duty after the capture of a port.


The German staff officers assured the
correspondent that the German COM
mander, Gen. Won Beseler, had found
easy victory in his campaign, where
hard fighting was expected and desper-
ate resistance where little trouble had
been anticipated The officers said
Antwerp had fallen eight days earlier
than expected, the Belgians evidently
being disheartened by their nine weeks
of defeat, and also because OF the easy
manner in which the fortified positions
behind the River Nethe were carried
October 6 and Z.


AS the correspondent drove through
miles of the streets of Antwerp the
city seemed to have suffered less from
the bombardment than had been be-
lieved. Indications of damage wrought
by the German shells were observed in
all quarters of the city, but the de-
struction usually was confined to in
dividua1 houses at widely scattered
points, the great mass of intervening
buildings being untouched.


Heaviest of Guns Not Used.


At the German headquarters it was
said this fact was due to the definite
plan of the Germans to convince Ant
werp with a minimum of damage that
the city was at the mercy of their
guns and that further resistance was
useless. The heavy twelve and sixteen
inch guns, it was stated, were not used
against the city proper, but shells from
me smaller mortars We're dropped
throughout the place, a few in each
section until every quarter had been
systematically visited


How accurately the public buildings
were avoided seemed to have been
proved by shell hole in the pavement
and in the destruction of a house
across the street from that building.
The Church of Our Lady, the pride Of
antwerp. Al has a hole eight or ten feet





and in an adjoining wall thirty feet
above the floor. Otherwise this edifice
was not damaged.


The artillery park of the Germans
before Antwerp was stronger than was
generally known. In addition to their
widely heralded sixteenth mortars
ana large number of twelye-inch
siege guns they had two Austrian auto
mobile batteries of twelve guns


Outer Forts Badly DAMAGED.


The effect of the big guns on Ant
werp's outer Notifications was more
striking than at Liege. Two armored
turrets at Fort de Wavre-St Catherine
were put out of action with a single
shot. their steel beds being broken in
two and the heavy masses of metal
hurled five or six yards away. In an
oeher rort the concrete embankment
was pierced like an egg shell and the
steel turret uprooted. Still another tur-
ret was completely appended and lies
with its base pointing skyward and it's
gun buried beneath. ! ~,i7., = :, = :


Behind Fort Waelhem, where. a
tweive-inch shell penetrated the maya
zine, q heavy steam. engine which fur
nished power for the light plant was

entire top of the fort here was torn
Off and sixty men of the garrison are

German staff officers say that when
the River Nethe was crossed the Bel
g1an defense virtually collapsed. The

mans 1ntrenched' themselves, expecting

LONDON, Sept 10.--The following
official statement was given out to-
night:


The Colonial Secretary received to-
day two messages from the Governor
OF Nyassaland, dated yesterday. The
first says that on Tuesday the main
British force advanced with the inten-
ton OF driving back the enemy across
the frontier. The enemy, apparently
about 1000 strong. evaded the British
force and at sunrise Wednesday at
tackled karonga, which was defended by
one officer and fifty African rifles and
police and eight civilians.


After three hours resistance one of
the columns OF the main British forces
arrived and drove off the enemy. The
full British force was engaging the
enemy when the Governors first mes
sage was despatched.


The second message stated that the
British field force had been heavily en-
gagged throughout the day. The enemy
fought with great determination and
had to be dislodged by repeated bayo-
net charges. They we're ultimately
driven across the Songwe. The British
force was too exhausted 20 pursue.


THE enemy lost seven officers killed
and two wounded and captured. Their
loss of the rank and file Is not as yet
exactly ascertained. but it is heavy.
Two field and two macKne guns were
captured from the enemy. The British
loss was four officers killed and seven
wounded. The loss in the rank and file
has not yet been definitely ascertained"

The name Of the woman who wrote
Aud Robin Gray" can never be for
gotten, for OF all Scotch songs and bal
lads there is none that has a greater ap-
peal than this. Lady Anne Barnard.
who wrote this when she was a young
woman, was born December s. 175O She
was the oldest daughter of the fifth Earl
OF Balcarres. Her early life was passed
in comparative retirement on her faith
er's estates in Scotland, and, save for
occasional winter flights to Edinburgh
where she met many prominent English
and Scotch people Of the day, she had
very little intercourse with society. Lady
Anne persistently refused to marry till
Andrew Barnard asked for her hand
when she was forty-three. He was con-
siderably younger than she was and
only his accomplishments and his charm
Of manner offset the fact that he was
poor and possessed few prospects With
him Lady Anne went to live in the Cape
Of Good Hope, where his business called
him, and for fourteen years they passed
a happy life. Then on his death Lady
Anne returned to England and lived in
London with her sister. In their Lon
don house they received the most bril-
liant literary society of the day, includ-
ing Burke and Sheridan. The Prince of

Wales was one Of Lady Anne's greatest
admirers, and this was whispered not
always to her credit.


In the meantime the Scotch ballad
"Auld Robin Gray had been published
for many years and was already a great
favorite. Several Scotchmen, including
a clergyman. had claimed II as their
production. Then, two years before her
death, Lady Anne wrote q letter to Sir
Walter Scott, who was a great admirer
of this simple little song, telling him
that she had written it The old Scotch
air, she told him, was a childhood IA
vorite Of hers, but because the original
words that went with the air were ex-
ceedingly indelicate she had had a de-
sire to compose her own words to tbs
favorite air. So 1t was that she wrote
the simple lines that have since noada
her name celebrated. She published tbe
poem anonymously, and II was not tin
she was seventy-three years old that she
revealed her secret authorship.

PHILADELPHIA, August 1O.-Captain,
crew and negro cook were still in some
what nervous condition when the Pawnee
Of the Clyde line docked here yesterday.
They had been as close as they wish
to being blown out of the water by the
dreadnought Florida and the torpedo
boat destroyer Drayton


Saturday night about o'clock Capt
Rich headed his ship toward the outer
New York harbor. The negro cook had
food box in the pantry and had gone
on deck for whiff of air Moored near
the Narrows was the Florida, her, decks
alive with white-clad sailors. The skip
per of the Pawnee, like all good sailors,
gave the Florida wide berth. The cook
waved to the sailor boys aboard Uncle
Sans fighting machine. but probably, in
the dusk of the evening, was not seen.
Then the Florida focused its powerful
searchlight on the Pawnee. A moment
later a shot from one of it's guns went
over the Pawnees bow.


Skipper Ignorant of Rule.


''That's fine," mused Capt. Rich. He
didn't think the shot was intended to
halt him. The Pawnee's quartermaster
held his course. and a second shot from
tho Florida tipped across the bow.


The negro cook has no fear of sen
storm, and cares not a whit for reckless
chauffeurs when he's on shore leave
but when those solid shot went singing
across the ships nose the deck ceased
to have any attraction for him. He re-
tired to the galley.


About that time Capt. Rich saw black
smoke curling from the smokestacks of
the Drayton, which soon speeded down
the Narrows in the Pawnee's wake
Capt. Rich decided then and there that
his little 1.20O-ton ship would not be pass
ed by the audacious craft manned by
gentlemen with white duck uniforms and
patent leather shoes.


Chased for Five Miles.


It was a nice little chase for five miles,
and when the DTayton overhauled the
Pawnee Capt. Rich was ordered to go
about and comply with the new port
regulations, that every outgoing vessel
must pass near the Florida and make
known her identity. The PaWnee com
piled with the regulation.


Uncle Sam is taking no chances on
contraband or European reservists being
shipped from New York.


Capt Pinkham of the Start Point a
British frigate steamship that arrived In
this port yesterday. told how he was
compelled to exercise unusual vigilance
in the voyage across the Atlanuc 10
avoid German cruisers.


The Start Point sailed from London
seventeen days ago.

important news today would instantly get
out an extra edition, for the whole country
was waiting patiently for word that peace
had been concluded.

PANAMA. June 21.-The canal terminal Is
at Balboa and Cristoba1 have now become
regular ports of call for several steamship
lines. Interruption of the Tehuantepec
railway route across southern Mexico
drove considerable shipping to these
ports, but even now, with the Tehuante-
pee service re-esta ablished, there are many
boats which continue to call at Balboa
or Cristobal for transfer of cargo across
the isthmus. The American-Hawaiian
Steamship Company has gone back to the
Mexican ports. but only until the canal
is ready for regular use. The Elder and
Fyfe Company. however, which has hith-
erto had only an occasional service be-
tween Liverpool and Cristobal. has now
increased its service and is running regu-
lar steamships. and Norwegian line of
tramp steamers calls regularly, while on
the west coast ports the Salvadorian rail-
way steamship line has been diverted
from Mexican ports to Balboa

new Japanese line will begin service to

Antwerp, Oct. 19.-0n his arrival in
Antwerp the correspondent of The As
sociated Press found guarding the city


bluejackets and marine infantrymen


from the German stations at Kiel,
Cuxhaven and Wilhelmshaven. They
were smelling the salt water after a
campaign of more than a month
through Belgium and awaiting further
orders.


Detacf ments Of sailors among them,
recruited from the German mercantile
marine, were armed only with cut
lass and revolver. They had lain sew
eral weeks behind the army, taking no
part in the fighting, and evidently are
destined for sea duty after the capture
of port.


The German staff officers assured the
correspondent that the German com
mander, General Won Beselcr, in his
campaign had found easy victory
where hard fighting was expected and
desperate resistance where little trou-
bic had been anticipated. The officers
said Antwerp had fallen eight days
earlier than expected, the Belgians
evidently being disheartened by their
nine weeks of defeat and also because
of the easy manner in which the forti-
fed positions behind the River Nethe
were carried on October 8 anc p


The artillery park of the Germans
before Antwerp was stronger than was
generally known. In addition to their
widely ,heralded 16-inch motars and n
large number of 12-inch siege guns,
they had two Austrian automobile bat
teries of twelve guns. which made the
victory at Antwerp an Austro-German
one.


The effect of the big guns at Ant
wcrp's outer Notifications was more
striking than at Liege. Two armored
turrcts at Fort de Wavre-Ste Catherine
we're put out of action with a single
shot, their steel beds being broken in
two and the heavy masses of metal
hurled five or six yards away In an
other fort the concrete embankment
was pierced like an egg she'll and the
steel turrot uprooted. Still another
turret was completely upended and lies
with its base pointing skyward and it's
gun buried beneath.


Behind Fort Waelhem, where a IL
inch she'll penetrated the magazine, n
heavy steam engine which furnished
power for the light plant was blown
twenty yards from its base. The en-
tire top Of the fort here was torn off
and sixty men Of the garrison are said
70 have been buried underneath the
debris.


German staff officers say that when
the River Nethe was crossed the Bel
gian defence virtually collapsed. The
Belgians abandoned their heavy artil
lery and machine guns while the Ger
mans intrenched themselves, expecting
q counter attack.


The officers say that after eighty
German shells had been dropped in
various quarters of the city of Ant
werp the white flags appeared on Forts
G and Of the inner girdle of fortifca-
tions. The Burgomaster of the city
then came out and offered to surrender
Antwerp, but was told that the terms
Of capitulation could only be conducted
with the Belgian military authorities.
The Burgomaster's plea that these Of
fcers could not be found led to an
order for a suspension of the attack.


The German troops then pushed in
the girdle of inner forts and
past the undefended city wall, finding
that the retiring garrison had blown
up the bridge across the River Scheldt
and also had interposed a belt of fame
against the invaders by firing the oil
tanks and covering the surface of the
river with burning oil.

It is now admitted. however, that In

withstanding the hardships of the winter

VALPARAISO, Nov. G.


There is little hope remaining in VAL
paraiso that Rear Admiral Sir Christo-
pher Cradock his flagship the Good Hope
and the 300 men of her crew survived
the first great naval engagement of the
war, when, on Sunday evening, German
fleet sank the Monmouth and scattered
the other units of the British cruiser
squadron


Whether the Glasgow and the Otranto,
which escaped destruction. survived the
damage suffered is not known. The
whereabouts of the German cruisers
Leipzig and Bremen also remains in
doubt.


Contrary to first reports, the Good
Hope and Glasgow did not reach Coronel
or Talcahuano, nor did the Otranto find
a Chilan port. The German fleet, with
the exception Of the Leipzig and the
Bremen, after putting in here, left again.
If they had any word of the Leipzig and
the Bremen they did not make it known.
The transport Prinz Eitcl anchored In
the bay last night


A wireless cry from the British cruiser
Glasgow-intercepted by the German
victors-was the last word received from
Rear Admiral Cradock's squadron, follow
ing the engagement off the Chilian coast
Sunday.


The Germans saw the Monmouth sink
and heard an explosion on board the
Good Hope that they believe sent the
crippled flagship to the bottom.


All that night the German cruiser
Nuruberg searched the seas for the Good
Hope unsuccessfully. They picked up
radiosram directed to the flagship by
the Glasgow. There was no reply.


At the moment that the German guns
were trained the Good Hope was seen
coming at full speed and through good
seamanship she managed to join the
other British ships The British had
come about and the two squadrons
steamed southwark in parallel lines, the
Germans being closer to the coast Grad
ually the two lines came nearer to each
other and the Scharnhorst and the Gnei-
senau simultaneously let go their u S-nch
guns, which they concentrated on the
Good Hope. The firing continued for
several minutes without damage. The
German shots fell short, and the Good
Hope had such roll that she could not
reply. The small cruisers were far out
of range.


Slowly the vessels drew nearer, and
when the two units were but COCO yards
apart the Good Hope fired her two 9-inch
guns. She was still unable to use her
eight 6-inch guns. which on the gun deck
were so near the water line that as the
vessel rolled they were almost awash
a terrible broadside from the Scharn-
horst and the Gneisenau crippled the Brit
ish flagship and her engines stopped.
The Monmouth. recognizing the distress
of her companion, made a dash to cover
the Good Hope. but by that time the
distance separating the two squadrons
had been reduced to 5000 wards. and the
Germans were able to bring all their
ships into action and TO use all the guns

NEW YORK, August 17.-Sir Thomas
Lipton's Shamrock ", challenger for the
Americas cup. ended her long trans
Atlantic journey last night, reaching
New York harbor shortly before mid
night. The Shamrock came in under
tow of Sir Thomas Lipton's steam yacht
Erin. The cup yacht Is on this side Of
the water to be laid up for the winter
Meanwhile the European war had
broken out. and the Shamrock lay in
harbor at Bermuda while the New York
Yacht Club, holders of the Americas cup,
were deciding that because of the Eu-
ropean conflicts the races should be put
over until next year.


With that decision made the Sham
rock and her convoy put out from Ber-
muda Thursday last for New York. A
wireless message from the Erin while the
two craft were still some distance out
side Sandy Hook said they would put
in at a late hour and remain down the
bay overnight.


All on board were reported well.
Sailing master and crew were greatly
disappointed because the cup yacht races
would not be sailed this year. They in
sisted that the Shamrock was in excel
lent shape to give a good account of
herself.


1t is understood that Sir Thomas yacht
Erin, which conveyed the Shamrock, sent
a wireless message today to the German
thanking the station for Its unwilling
assistance in enabling the Shamrock to
dodge German war craft. By picking
up messages intended for German cruis-
ers the Erin was warned Of their prox-
unity.

Two resolutions providing for investi-
cations into the oil business of the United
States, particularly the Standard Oil
Company, were unanimously adotped by
the Senate yesterday.


One Of the resolutions, offered by-Sena-
tor Gore, of Oklahoma, calls for a search
ing investigation by the Federal Trade
Commission, when appointed, into the
operations of the Standard OIL Company
and the companies into which the Stan
dard was divided following the decree of
dissolution by the Supreme Court. The
resolution seeks to determine Just what
connection, II any, now exists between
the Standard and these companies and
whether they are cooperating to injure
Independent oil companies.


The second resolution adopted was that
introduced by Senator Chiffon. of West
Virginia, calling for an investigation by
the Interstate Commerce Commission
into the conditions existing in the oil
business in New York. Pennsylvania
West Virginia, Ohio. Oklahoma and else
where. The resolution was offered be-
cause it was charged that the Standard
Oil Company, following the opening of
the war in Europe, has purchased only
about 25 per cent Of the oil it formerly
purchased from independent producers in
the Appalachian fields.

The Los Angeles-Phoenix race is gen.
orally conceded to be the hardest and
most dangerous race in the world. No
course has ever been selected that
proved such a terrific grind as the 7O6
miles covered by the drivers between
these cities on November 9, 10 and IL.


For hundreds OF miles the road winds
over the burning desrt sands, cut deep
with ruts and hollows and chuck holes.
in some places so narrow that two cars
cannot pass. Sharp rocks, big boulders
and cactus are strewn everywhere.


over mountain ranges that rise 1000
feet, through mountain passes where the
road hangs over sheer precipiceS thou
sands of feet deep, plunging down roads
that drop 1900 feet in ten miles into
dark canyons. Through dried-up river
beds and up steep banks made by deep
washouts.


This was the seventh time the Cactus
Derby was run. The course chosen was
the most difficult 5O6 miles. Both cars
and drivers were put to a test that no
other race, not even the six previous
Cactus Derby races, have ever exacted.


Twenty cars started. Among them can
be numbered the best that are produced
anywhere. Only eight survived, and
many OF these came in on their last legs,
tottering over the finished line. bent and
broken.


The first car to speed over the finished
line in Phoenix was Nikrent in a Paige
''36'; second was Oldfield in his StutZ
racing machine, the latter, however hav-
ing an advantage In elapsed time which
made him the winner by 81 minutes p
seconds


This car driven by Barney Oldfeld
is the same special racing machine that
was built 10 compete in the 50O-mile In
dlanapolis race and in the Elgin Trophy
race.


The most remarkable feature OF all in
connection with the two Paige entries
was the fact that Nikrent's car. which
finished in second place. never had the
hood removed during the entire three
days. and both Paige cars did not eXpe-
rience the slightest tire trouble during
the entire race. The greatest surprise
was the result of the remarkable con-
sistency shown by the Paige entries in
spite Of the absolutely different methods
adopted by the two drivers as their rae
ing schedule.


Nikrent set himself the task OF driv-
ing the entire race at an average speed
of thIrty-one miles per hour, saving his
car over the good stretches. and exact
ing every ounce OF power, speed and
endurance over the bad stretches. On
the contrary Beaudet worked on the
exact opposite principle, having decided
at the very beginning to open her wide
and drive his car to the limit every foot
Of the way. and though the punishment
the car and he must have suffered was
almost unendurable. the results due to
what was In the car itself brought him
in right behind Nikrent.


The honor has ben accorded the cars
for the most consistent performance IN
the history Of the Cactus Derby race.

A mixed grill is very popular in Eng
land for luncheon. but it would be as good
as light dinner or supper.


The following recipe makes enough for
three persons: Three lamb chops. one
half pound of sausages. four kidneys.
two tomatoes and a half pound Of mush-
rooms. Grill the chops. sausages and
kidneys together. slice the tomatoes and
fry with the mushrooms. The mush-
rooms and the tomatoes should not be
cooked long enough for the slices of to-
matoes to lose their shape. Arrange the
meat on a platter. lay the vegetables
around the edge. garnish with parsley
and serve No gravy should be used
with this dish, not even the juice from
the mushrooms and tomatoes. or the
flavor will be spoiled and the grill will
look messy and unappetizing.


Try this recipe some time when you
have few sausages or kidneys left over
from some meal. and you will find that
you have new and excellent dinner
dish with very little trouble or expense.

hall, where the German flag was hoisted

Dover tvia London, Dec. 22. Brit
ish warships have been doing effective
work in bombarding German positions
along the Belgian coast. They have
time after time made the voyage
across the North Sea. engaged posi-
tions that the Germans had strongly
fortified, destroyed batteries, caused
great loss of life among the enemy's
troops and returned safely to port.
These operations have had particular
value in the destruction, or partial de-
struction, Of the submarine base the
Germans were creating at IeebrUgge.


The destruction of German batteries
in a radius of several miles inland
has enabled the allied troops 20 make
appreciable advances in the last few
days. Some of the batteries which
we're engaged at the week end were
mounted two or more miles inland and
consisted of heavy guns. A gratifying
feature Of these operations has been
the fact that remarkably few casual
ties were sustained on the warships
The German submarines on several oc-
casions endeavored to make their pres
ence felt during these bombardments,
but the destroyers very effectively pro-
tected the heavier vessels and drove off
the attacking submarines.


II is feature well worth noting
that the Germans have never attempted
to attack the bombarding fleet from the
sea except by submarines. and the Ger
man army has not been able to obtain
the least assistance from the powerful
German navy while this destruction of
positions on their right wing and the
disastrous loss of life accompanying
it has been proceeding.

eastern roads have been increased,
their conditions could be bettered
without cutting too deeply into the


roads profits.

several weeks ago showed 1872 per
! cent of the men in favor OF a strike
! unless their demands are granted. The
territory that would be affected II the
strike was called extends from Lake
Michigan TO the Pacific coast and
from the Mexican border into Canada,

portance in the west.

AS said in advertisement of August 18th,
lit is very good these days to be an American"
During this month our country has encountered
trying experience in which our finances, our
foreign trade and even our domestic business
have been disturbed by the sudden and tremen-
dOus wars in our ancestral countries.
Yet we are coming out Of it well.


The President, with his cabinet and the Congress,
and the cooperation of bankers and business
called to Washington for the purpose. have
promptly and nobly met the emergency by
sensible rulings and wise laws, which will largely
free industries and commerce from restraint.
They have arranged for the issuance of emergency
currency, through amendment of the Aldrich-
Vreeland Law, under which national banks
obtain all the currency needed for legitimate
business.


They have organized the Federal Reserve Board
which will insure the opening of the twelve
Federal Reserve Banks inside of sixty days, thus
giving ample banking facilities for business to
every section of our country.


They have amended the ship registry laws so that
American capital will buy foreign ships, which
together with the large number of ships already
owned by Americans, will fly the flag of the
United States and furnish ample carrying capac-
ty for our foreign trade.


They have opened the Panama Canal, and thus pro-
vided shorter routes for our commerce with South
America, Australia and the Far East.
They have under consideration plan Of financing
the surplus cotton crop so that our southern
planters will be enabled to hold their cotton until
normal markets are restored

SACRAMENTO. Cal. April 4.-Three
convicts Were shot and instantly killed
and two others wounded, probably fatal
ly, in an attempted break from the in
corrigibIe ward of Folsom prison today.
The dead are Jose Lucfrica. serving two
years for grand larceny: Earl W. Siprell,
serving two years for robbery: Raymond
Blade serving two years for burglary.


The fatally wounded Norman c. Hare.
serving two years for assault. shot
through body; Percy Barnes. serving two
years for grand larceny, shot through
body.


All five men were literally riddled with
bullets. Thirteen prisoners were in the
plot to escape, but not one reached the
outside of the building Prison officials
were prepared for the break, for the
guards of the ward had overheard the
convicts planning to escape Thursday
night The leaders in the plot were
warned not to attempt the break.


At a signal given by the ringleaders
the convicts broke through wooden doors
OF their cells and rushed into the cor
ridors. F. Outlet and E. c. Wiseback,
two of the guards. opened fire with rifles.
The incorrigible ward is a new building,
not entirely completed. Steel cage doors
have not yet been installed in the cells.


The first sound of breaking cell doors
the guards began shooting. Several of the
convicts were unable to get out of their
cells at the first rush. and when their
fellow prisoners began to fall, they made
no further effort to escape.

Denver. - According to P. Nc
Donough, acting section director of
the weather bureau, weather condi-
tions during the past week were gem
orally favorable to crop growth and
farming operations, and all crops
made satisfactory progress. The sun
shine was generally abundant and
temperature conditions were practical
ly normal. Although the rainfall was
generally less than the usual seasonal
average, frequent and beneficial
showers occurred over the entire
state, but at the close of the week
rain was needed in nonirrigated dis
tricts. The heavy rains of the pre-
ceding week damaged alfalfa in south
central countries. The harvesting of
the second crop of alfalfa is practical
ly finished and the third crop has had
an excellent start. Wheat is being
harvested and thrashed, the yield be-
ing exceptionally good. The condi-
ton of corn, sugar beets, potatoes, pas
lures, fruit, tomatoes and cantaloupes
is notably good. Pears and early vari-
eties of peaches are being shipped
from Western fruit districts.

Editor Of the New Yort German Journal


New York. Aug. &.-Among the leading
nations OF the world Germany is the
only one that has had no war for the
last forty -four years.


Russia and Japan were fighting only a
few years ago. Previous to that Japan
had her war with China, and Russia her
war with Turkey.


France and Italy had their wars in
Northern Africa. England had her
struggle with the Beers.


The United States and Spain were at
war in 1895. Portugal had a civil war.
Chile and Peru had their war. Austria
Hungary had the occupation Of Bosnia.
Mexico has been one large battlefield
for more than a year.


Germany alone among the big nations
Of the world has kept peace for forty
four years, and for twenty-six out of
these forty-four years a so-called War
lord has been the Emperor OF Germany.


Germany Denies Charge.


England, France. and Russia charge
Germany with having started a great
European war. Germany denies having
been the aggressor.


History will decide this point, and in
the meantime II behooves Americans TO
reserve their Judgment Prussia sent US
Friedrich Wilhelm Won Steuben to or
ganize the, army that finally drove the
British from these shores.


Germans have helped 10 build up Ameri
can cities, they have cultivated American
sell. they have established many bust
nesses, encouraged commerce. fostered art,
and promoted civic righteousness. They
have always been loyal defenders Of their
adopted Countrywide United States.


Every reader Of papers personally
knows some Germans. He works side
by side with them. trades with them.
meets them in the street, in church, In
clubs, in every walk OF life.


The Germans who have made America
their home are the same ordinary. every
day human beings as their brothers and
cousins now fighting in Europe for their
hearths and homes, their mothers, wives,
and children.


The Germans who are struggling for
the very existence Of their country are
the same ordinary, sociable human be-
ings as the average home-loving Ameri-
cans who are proud OF their country and
ready to fight for its flag.


Americans have no reason to hate Ger
mans or Germany. The United States
has had two wars with England and does
not hate the British people. America had
no war with Germany. so IT has still less
cause for nl will toward Germany.


Americans will be neutral in the true
sense of the word. They will not pass
Judgment before they have had a full
hearing. Let US remain strictly impartial
with malice toward none and charity
for ALL

Vera Cruz, April 24.-Old Vera
Cruz is beginning to emerge from the
battle of the last two days. Shutters
are opening, dark-eyed, indolent
women with their hair hanging down
their backs are leaning from quaint
balconies and little tables under the
arcades around the plaza are again
filled with a curious, cosmopolitan
crowd taking their refreshments.


There was some sniping during the
night, but it was quiet to-day. with
blueiackets and marines policing every
block. Admiral Fletcher's proclama-
ton in Spanish, assuring the people
that the occupation is temporary and
civil officers shall continue their regu-
lar duties, was tackled up and read by
bewildered natives everywhere. There
are many of those quaint, serio-comic
little dramas inevitable i'll such
clash between people who do not I'M
derstand each others speech nor ways
OF thinking.


No stranger battle was ever fought
than that of the last two days. Navy
losses were ten times greater than in
the battle of Santiago, yet this is not
war. While Mausers were cracking from
housetops and closed shutters yester-
day the young officers and men march
ing against an enemy they could not
see, the Mexican transport Zaragoza,
damned with reinforcements, steamed
into the harbor under the very guns OF
the Dreadnoughts, any one OF which
could have crushed it as if it were
mosquito.


AS this is not war, the vessel could
not even be detained, but was ordered
not to anchor and, greatly to the
chagrin of the hapless Federal soldiers
on board no doubt, put about and
wandered aimlessly to sea again.

The prohibition movement had its origin in the
fact that on July /, 1862, the government imposed
tax upon alcoholic liquors and thus legalized the

this action crystallized in convention of 500 dele
gates in Chicago although in several States, notably
Illinois and Michigan, local prohibition organizations

didate named in 1872.


In some respects the prohibition movement re-
sembles the anti-savery crusade. Its leaders have
been imbued with righteous zeal Their agitation has
been persistent The literature in favor of prohbi-
ton would in itself, form large library, while the
discussion of the subject before Good Government
leagues and similar organizations, fill many volumes.
The evil of the drink habit has been portrayed in
brilliant colors. While have been made the
fact is that the extreme and radical views advanced
have hampered the growth of the Prohibition party.
More people believe in regulation than in absolute
prohibition and this belief is based upon the fact that
prohibition does not prohibit. The State of Maine,
where prohibition was adopted exactly sixty-three
years ago. has not yet abolished the liquor traffic
within its borders and not long ago it was necessary
to appoint commission to determine how the anti
liquor laws could be enforced


The Prohibitionists have always contended that
participation in politics the best method of ac-
complishing their desired ends Their platform for
1912 declared that to destroy the liquor traffic there

THE first report that the Treaty Of Client
i had been completed and peace estao-
lished with Great Britain reached Philadel-
phia in a most mysterious manner and fully
a week before Washington had official ad-
vices. AS we expect to celebrate the cen
tennial anniversary of the conclusion of the
peace of Client this year. this little known
story may be of interest now.


The treaty was signed on Christmas Eve,
1914 but sailing vessels did not cross the
Atlantic in those days with the speed of
modern ocean liners and there was neither
cable nor wireless to transmit the news.
However, early in the year 1916 a mysterious
stranger called upon President Madison at
Washington one evening and brought him
the news


That night this same mysterious stranger
sent letter to John Binns who published
the Democratic Press in this city, giving
him the same news. Probably no modern
newspaper owner would have done what
Binns did. Any newspaper receiving such
important news today would instantly get
out an extra edition for the whole country
was waiting patiently for word that peace
had been concluded.

NEW YORK, Feb. 1.-the attend
ance in broker Offices and on the
Stock Exchange was light day,
owing TO the blizzard conditions that
prevailed all day. No important spec
ulative influence was forthcoming
from Europe, where quiet week end
conditions prevailed. Americans were
slightly changed in either direction
abroad, and foreigners showed no dis
position to trade in this market, but
that is not unusual for a Saturday.


The market opened quiet and lrreg-
ularly changed. Amalgamated Cop
per, Reading and New York Central
were a shade higher in the intia!
transactions. while Union Pacific.
Southern Pacific and United States
Steel were fractionally lower. The
latter assumed prominence immedi-
ately after the opening, however, and
moved up on active professional buy
ing. The strength in the steel issues
Influenced the entire list sympathet-
ically. Rock Island issues were about
the only notable exception to the re
covery in the early trading.


The closing half of the session was
marked by uncertainty, but prices
moved within a narrow range. The
dealings were largely by the trading
element. T short depression in Ca
madam Pacific and heaviness in Rock
Island were the features.

a truck in the garage of the Milwaukee
Casket Company. Alma Leopold, seven
teen years old, and Fred Oehler, her
sweetheart. carried out what the police
believe was a suicide pact today.


Employees broke down the locked doors

a bullet wound in her head, lying beside
the truck. Sitting in the front seat Of
the truck one lifeless hand still gripping
the wheel, they found Oehler, who was
an employe OF the company. There was
a powder SCARED bullet wound on the
right side of his head. A revolver and
bottle of poison lay at his feet.


Two notes, in different handwriting.
were found on an order blank of the
company. They read:


kindly notify Edward Straus. Phone
coroner. Thanks for this favor and for
all past favors-Fred Oehler.''


Kindly notify Mrs. H. Leopold.-Alma
Leopold"


The girls body was stiffened and cold,
showing that she had been dead several
hours. Oehler's body was warm, indi-
eating that he killed himself but a few
minutes before the bodies were found.

REDDING, Cal, September 21.-After
night of muttering and rumbling.
Lasson peak exploded today in a sharp
thunderclap. which rocked the houses
at Macomber Flat. distant nine miles
from the mountain.


The eruption today is the forty
eighth since the prehistoric volcano
awoke to life May 80. and the first that
has been accompanied by an EARTH
quake.


At the time the shock was felt-3
o'clock in the morning-the activities
of the mountain were not pronounced
enough to make themselves visible
from a distance, but at 6 o'clock a
vast volume of sulphurous. ash-laden
smoke and steam was seen pouring
from a fssure one mile below the
older vents.


The mountain now has four craters-
the ancient one, still sealed: the new
main crater. adjacent: a third crater
formed by the eruptions of the last
three weeks not far below the main
crater, and the f1ssure blown open
today.


Twice yesterday the new craters
spouted clouds of smoke, but today
they were inactive, while the lower
vent was furiously busy. Smoke and
floating ashes veiled the entire noun
tainside.

fragists.

LUXEMBOURG, Grand Duchy of Lux
emburg, November II, via The Hague
and London, November 12.-This small
country, which has almost been forgot
ten since the commencement of the
war, is beginning to show signs of un-
rest under the prolonged German rule.


Entirely cut off from the rest of the
world and obliged to read newspapers
which under a strict German censor
ship are giving exclusively pro-German
information. the people show the same
to fly into panics and to be-
lieve historical news as are SO familiar
in Brussels, Liege, Namur and other
Belgian cities, where the people sys-
tematically are kept in the dark. They
are willing now to believe even the
most incredible rumors.


Suffer From the War.


The Luxemburgians have suffered
greatly since the Germans three weeks
ago stopped the iron industry, the
main support of the country. by forbid
ding the use of dynamite. After pro-
longed negotiations the operation of
the mines has been allowed again. but
the miners are obliged to use other and
less violent explosives.


Continual friction is apparent between
the Luxemburgians and the Germans
on the frontier villages. The people
who ordinarily are bi-lingual, under
pressure of the unlimited Germans nov
are using French exclusively, as the
only means at their disposal of show
.ountry's invasion and continued domi-
nation,

says:


AT the opening of the week moder-
ate to heavy rain fell over the greater
part OF the state east of the noun
tains. These rains were timely and
fell over sections of the state where
most needed. Fairly well distributed
showers occurred in the counties on
the Western slope. The moisture was
generally ample for crop growth. Tenn
perature conditions were practically
normal in the eastern half of the
state; in the western half the weather
was somewhat cooler than the season
al average. The days were warm and
the sunshine abundant; the nights,
however, were relatively cool.

conditions have been favorable and
crops have made satisfactory progress.
Some damage has been caused by hail,
especially in Boulder county. Alfalfa
in localities in the western part of the
state has been beaten down by wind
and rain, but the damage has not been
great. Sugar beets are making rapid
growth, also small grain. Garden
truck, corn and potatoes are doing
well. Cutting of the first crop of al
falfa is progressing rapidly, the quail
ity as well as the yield being good.
Early fruits are being gathered in
the southwestern part of the state.

Never again the war-wise face.


The weighed and urgent word,
That pleaded in the marketplace,


Pleaded and was not heard.
Yet from life new life aprings


Through all the hosts to come,
And glory is the least OF things

NEW YORK, November 5.--The first
thought that comes in this new de-
mand for cotton frocks Is the excep-
tionally lovely ones worn by our imme-
date ancestors. those frilly affairs Of
cotton net and organdie and val lace.
Why not revive them?


Cotton crepe is all very we'll for an
informal house frock and the ginghams
and calicoes that the artistic members
Of the patriotic southerners have adopt
ed for every day use in ones own heat
ed rooms are admirable and colorful
for just that purpose, but for evening
wear the fine organdie and cotton mus
lin are the best choice.


These are made all the more wear
able by the new fashion which calls
for ruff1es on the skirt and a bodice
without sleeves and cut on less formal
lines than those which have prevailed
for years. Even the great Callot lends
her art in September to frocks that
were nothing more or less than a
shower of flounces, often edged with
colored taffeta in the fashion of the
carly sixties.


At one Of the smart dances among
the younger set here, an informal
countryside affair. the hostess found a
gown that had served in a tableau some
years ago which had been made after
the hoopskirt, uncovered shoulder Pc
Rod, the fabric of fine cotton net, the
fiounces edged with blue ribbon. She
saw how nearly it resembled a Callot
frock her young aunt had brought from
Paris during wartime, and freshening
1t up a bit, she tucked in pink rose,
added white stockings and laced fat
heeled black satin slippers and found
herself the envy of the dancers.


She had done that wonderful thing
among women; she had invented new
style. or rather different style, and
she received due tribute.

The heroism Of Arthur Cleveland,
motorman of the Westchester & Bos-

responsible for his death yesterday In
the White Plains Hospital.


With Clyde Holcombe, Cleveland
went TO the Heathcote station early
Yesterday morning and got an electric
ear 10 take out an oil tank car from
the siding there. The iron handle OF
the pump struck the heavily charged
wires and Holcombe received full in
his body the force Of 1000 volts. lie
was hurled a hundred feet and killed
instantly. Cleveland was hurled forty
feet, his clothing almost entirely
stripped from him and his left arm
broken.


Despite his injuries he tried to nelo
his friend. Finding that HOlcombe was
dead, Cleveland then struggled back TO
the car, drove il mile 70 tell tower
man what had happened and then drove
il back TO the Heathcote siding, elea~-
ing the line for the express trains
bringing the New York theatregoers,
the first of which was nearly due.


He was carried 20 the hospital at
White Plains, where he died late in the
afternoon. Had he received treatment
earlier il is possible that he would have
lived. His home was in New Rochelle.

Paris, Sept. l9.-The honors OF the air
are about even In the, campaign so far.
Perhaps a little advantage lies with the
invaders. But the Zeppelin, the great
German dirigibles, have proved of little
use except in bomb throwing.
The English and French have learned
a great deal about the enemies move
ments with their own dirigible balloons,
although these have not been used for
bomb-throwing. The aeroplane service
Of both sides is so highly developed that
the surprise attack has been practically
eliminated from warfare.


Sir John French in an Official report
praises his Reroplane squadron and de-
clares that they have kept him con-
stantly informed Of the movements of
the Germans. The French fast mono
planes make long journeys to Germany
and the German Taubes penetrate far
into the interior of France.


The war has proved ehat an aeroplane
flying a nile high is practically safe
from both rifles and artillery. Not one
hit Is made in 5000 or 1000 shots. and
when reaching its mark the spent bullet
usually infiicts only minor damage. The

Washington. March 1S.-The Earring note
OF Mexico was again sounded in the SEN
ate to-day when the Urgent Deficiency
bill. containing an appropriation Of 500 600
for feeding Mexican soldiers and refugees
who have been driven across the border
and are now detained by the United
states. came up for discussion.


Senator Bristow declared that the
United States was taking upon itself an
obligation which would never be repaid,
spending many hundred thousand dollars
upon MeXicans who were treated as bel
ligerents without recognizing formally the
belligerency of either the Huerta or the
Carranza faction Senator Smoot in
sisted that notice should be given TO
the United states would not continue to
feed the women and children who accom-
panied the Mexican army which fed
across the border.


Senators Martin and Overman explained
that the United States was bound by the
Hague convention TO observe its neutral
itv obligations by disarming the soldiers
who crossed the border and keeping them
under surveillance until hostilities were at
an end Senator Lodge took the same
view. but contended that the obligation
did not extend 20 the civilian refugees.
To meet this objection the Senate adopted
an amendment specifying that the appro-
praticn should be expended for mill
tary' refugees


How to distinguish between military
and non-miltary refugees was the next
question to perplex the Senate The prob
lem was finally left for the state and
War departments TO solve and the appro-
priation was authorized.

she thinks her daughter went away for

Il dreaded the publicity" Mrs. Blu

Mrs Buchanan has been expecting a

anticipated message would bring news Of
a marriage, but this morning when no
word had been received, Mrs. Buchanan
stated, she was unable to bear the
suspense any longer.


A week ago last Sunday, stated Mrs.
Buchanan. young man called at the
house to see her daughter and was in
troduced to her. 1t was the first time she
had seen him. she said. and she thinks he
probably has gone away with the missing
high school pupil.


Miss Buchanan was at home with her





She assisted in household work and SEEM
ed bright and CHEEKY, and Friday morn
ing when she left home, ostensibly to go
to school, there was nothing about her
conduct to suggest anything out of the
ordinary She was able to conceal care
fully any plans for leaving home perma-
nently.


Took Belongings With Her.


1t was not until after the young lady
had left home at o'clock in the morn
ing that her mother discovered she had
taken her belongings with her. Practical
ly every garment the young lady pos
sessed and all her toilet articles were
gone, and she had not left a note to let
her mother know that she was going
where she would be in safe hands.


Mrs. Buchanan thinks her daughter
packed her belongings Thursday night
and that she threw them from window
to her supposed prospective husband.
She also thinks the young man may have
called in an automobile.


The missing high school pupil has dark
brown hair and eyes, and when she left
home Friday morning she wore a gray
dress and black hat and carried white
muff. Her description was telephoned to
the several police stations with request
that the police search for her, and the

ers again became fashionable.


The present Is an era OF fast over

idad Rodriguez was seriously wound

CONSTITUTIoNALIsT HEAD
QUARTERS. GOMEZ PALACIO.
MEXICO, March 2s.-Torreon prob
ably will fall before night. A des-
perate battle is being fought in the
streets of the city. The Federals are
fighting bravely to thrust back Villas
rebels. but the Constitutionalists are
slowly forcing their way into the
heart OF the town


The bombardment which General
Villa maintained all day Friday
ceased last night and the rebel com
mander gave the order for the at
tack. Crossing the Nazas River at
the head of HIS troops, Villa smashed
the Federal defenses' to the north and
penetrated the town.


Battle RACES All Night.


The battle ragged all night Neither
SIDE was able TO use its artillery in
the darkness, for fear Of killing its
own men. but the soldiers fought
hand-to- hand in the light cast by
fires burning in buildings set afre
early In the battle by the first bonn
VI


When the first light showed to-day
Villa sent into the battle all the
forces that he had held in reserve
during the night. Most Of these SOL
diers were the men who had been
given an opportunity to rest after the
battle that resulted in the capture OF
Gomez Palacio.


Fighting from the house tops and
from barricades III the streets the
Federals had succeeded during the
night in hurting back every attempt
of Villa to enter the principal plaza
Of the city. All night the Constitu-
tionalists had been cutting their way
through adobe houses for many blocks
In order to get behind the Federal
barbados. but the work was slow


Federal Commanders Slain.


General Villa sent a message TO his
headquarters here early this morning
confirming earlier reports that Gem
eral Ricardo Pena and Colonel Fred
erico Reyna, of the Federal army, had
been killed, and that General o. Car
rama and General Almanzan had
been fatally wounded. General Car
rama was the best cavalry leader
that the Federals had.


Villa stated that none OF his off,
GERS had been killed. but Colonel Trim
idad Rodriguez was seriously wound
ed. The rebel officers to-day admit
ted that 900 OF their men had been
killed In the fighting that resulted in
the capture Of Gomez Palacio. Five
hundred and fifty dead Federals have
been counted on the battlefield.

Dunkirk, Dec. SIN the dark hours
this morning the Germans hazarded
another desperate attack by armored
motor boats on the Belgian lines
southeast of Ramscapelle, near Per-
vyse.
Three powerful motor boats, fitted
with searchlights, approached within
two hundred metres of the Belgian
outposts. They towed a number OF
RATS, each holding fifty or sixty men.
Machine guns also were on the boats
and RATS. The first warning was given
TO the Belgians by the throb of the
motors. The alarm was at once given
and the Belgians opened fire in the di-
rection indicated by the noise of the
engines. At once the German search
lights flashed out on the Belgians and
a murderous fire began from the ma
chine guns on the RATS.


At first the Germans had the upper
hand, the binding glare Of their
searchlights dazzling the Belgians,
most of whose shots fell wide. The
bullets that struck the motor boats
did little harm against the armored
sides.


The Germans drew nearer. and were
preparing to land and rush the Bel
gians when the latter brought into play
one of their own searchlights, which
they hastily brought up from a posi-
ton quarter of mile behind the
lines. The German motor boats were
then more easily located, and the B.
gian gunners were able TO direct their
fire with some accurancy. For some
time this battle of searchlights ragged,
and as the great white beams fell on
the battling forces fantastic picture
was presented.


Gradually the Germans were driven
back. Those who still were on RATS,
unable to land and huddled together,
made On effective target for the Bel
gian guns. One of the German search
lights was put out by lucky shot, and
in the confusion which followed the
men on the raft attached TO the boat
carrying this light were pitched into
the water. They swan toward the Bel
gisns and gave themselves up as pris-
oners.


The Germans, however, continued to
work their machine guns, and the Bel
gians were unable to put them out Of
action. One motor boat then drew off
and a landing was attempted a few
hundred yards to the right Of where the
fighting was in progress in water knee
deep. The Germans took cover behind
the boat. The Belgians also advanced
in the water, and fierce struggle took
place for the possession of the boat.
With a great effort the Germans sue
ceeded in backing the craft out of dam
ger, and then drew off.


The third and last motor boat con-
tinued in action. and it might have
gone hard with the handful of Belgians
who were defending the line had not
the French 75-millimetre got the range.
When the first she'll fell into the water
all three motor boats at once swung
around and quickly disappeared. Two
Of them were badly damaged and APP
peared to be in a sinking condition.
The third was damaged slightly. The
losses on each side are believed to have
been about the same-about forty
killed and thirty wounded.

LONDON, June 5.-Miss Mary Blom-
field, daughter of Lady Sara Louisa
Bloomfield, widow of Sir Arthur Blom-
field. created a sensational scene at Buck
ingham Palace last night when she threw
herself on her knees before King George
and Queen Mary and started to make a
plea for the suffrage cause.


Miss Bloomfield alone was concerned
in the incident, although her sister. who
also attended the court. was requested
to leave the palace after the occurrence,
despite the fact that she took no part
in the demonstration. She left without
protest.


The father of Miss Bloomfield was a
well known architect Her grandfather
the late DIR. Bromfeld, was Bishop of
London. Lady Bloomfield. who attended
the function, explained today that she
was looking after a friend whom she
was presenting and that she saw nothing
Of her daughters action.


Officials of the palace today were on
the verge of nervous prostration as the
result of last nights scene. and the lord
chamberlain's department has taken
every precaution to circumvent any at
tempt to repeat the performance tonight
when another function takes place at
Buckingham Palace


Whole Scene Short Lived.


Persons in the immediate vicinity at
the time declare that the whole scene
lasted less than ten seconds, and that
the woman had only time to calculate
audibly, '.Your majesties. For COOS
sake when she was seized and -hus-
tied out of the throne room, finishing the
sentence as she went.


King George was the coolest man in the
company. and the presentations proceeded
after the incident with clockwork regu-
larity.


II is understood no further action will
be taken against Miss Bloomfield except
to bar her from future court functions
The sisters obtained admission to court
in the ordinary way through aDDiicauoi
to the lord chamberlain's department


Officials of the Women's Social and
Political Union, the militant organization,
deny responsibility for the incident at
Buckingham Palace.


Miss Bloomfield was attired In court
dress and her action caused consterna-
ton. AS she admoniShed the king the
conductor of the band in the gallery sig
nailed to the band to play louder ana
her voice was drowned.


The scene was so brief the assem-
blage generally had little knowledge OF
what was transpir1ng.


The police had knowledge of conspi-
racy to approach the royal presence ana
every guest and every carriage arriving
at Buckingham Palace had been sub
jected to close inspection by detectives.
an unusual precautiou and one that
caused considerable delay and not a
little indignation or irritation in court
circles.

Here Is a gripping story of q modern
day feud between two respected fami-
lies OF the South over disputed bound
ary line between their adjoining planta-
tons. II Is impossible to describe In Q
few words the rugged. strange and pic
turesque settings Of this ideal story OF
manhood elemental Not one dull mo-
ment will you find from start to finish.
The grudge fight; the accidental shooting
OF old Charlton's daughter; her recovery
and marriage to Jim Redfern. the son OF
her fathers bitterest enemy; and the re-
markable scene showing the Charlton
home in flames; and later the reunion
Of the warning families-these are but a
suggestion of the scenes that will quicken
your pulse and bring the unbidden tears. .


Briefly told. the story concerns the
long-standing warfare between the
Charltons and Redferns. Grace Charlton,
general favorite with everybody, is sent
to New York to study voice under the
leading teachers Of the metropolis Dur
ing her rise to fame and her subsequent
successful appearance In grand opera.

Redfern, who has completely won her by
his primitive wooing. Much as she loves
Jim, she does not hesitate to take sides
with her family against him when the
feud breaks out anew.

father has been wounded. and hastens
to her humble Southern home to direct
the fight for revenge waged by her broth
ers against the Redferns. Later. Grace
receives a bullet In her shoulder that was
intended for her father. The next night
the Charltons' home takes fire, and they
are rescued with great difficulty by old
man Redfern and his sons Jim Red
ferns heroism in rescuing Grace has
brought the feud to an end, and the story
closes with the marriage of Grace and
Jim, and the pact of friendship sealed
forever between the families OF Charlton
and Redfern.

The copious rains Of Saturday night
and Sunday which had not entirely
ceased today, benefited the farmers OF
Eastern Pennsylvania to the extent of
millions of dollars.


From agricultural sections within n
wide radius of Philadelphia come re-
ports all of the same tenor, jubilant
and optimistic. The precipitation was
steady, hour after hour. and the rain
Of warm temperature, just the sort for
which the farmer had been praying
through the period of drought which
had lasted for the greater part Of three
months, with only slight and widely
separated interruptions.


The rain Soaked" into the parched
earth, and its effect was scarcely short
of magical. In many places the ground
had been baked by the prolonged dry
spell, and when plowed, with the ut
most difficulty, the powdery substance
offered small hope of terminating the
seed. AS a result of the rainfall this
condition is changed, and from every
point comes the word that the yield OF
wheat and rye promises to equal the
usual dimensions.


Streams have been replenished, for
est fires quenched and in every view
the rain has been of immense value to
the agricultural and industrial inter-
ests. Reports from various districts,
printed below, give view of the wide
extent of the benefits of the downpour.

speed of about eight knots was

Definite news has reached Vancouver
that the Germans have captured the
Tanning Island cable station. Whether
the men who landed on the island
Monday, September Z, We're from the
cruisers Nurnberg or Leipzig cannot be
definitely ascertained. Communication
was broken off SO suddenly with the
Vancouver Island end of the cable that

men in uniform had landed, and had
entered the superintendent Office.
Here the message stopped abruptly,
and the cable has been silent ever
since.


Presumably the Germans Immediately
cut the cable at the shore end and took
off the coal and supplies that are
maintained OH the island for the use
of the cable operators.


Whether they took the operators as
prisoners of war is also unknown. 1t
is understood that the British admi-
rally are taking prompt steps to restore
communication with Australia and
New Zealand. Meanwhile business from
Great Britain and elsewhere is being
dispatched by the eastern route

the transcontinental telegraph across
Australia.
