PETROGRAD, Oct. 10.


The Russian War Office today an
nounced that Marggrabowa and Lyck,
two important railroad centres in East
Prussia, had been captured from the
Germans.


By making their attack on Marggra-
bowa from the southeast the Russians
forced the Germans to abandon their
fortified positions at Barkalezew on the
Rospula River, and Minister of War
Sukhominoff, who has returned from the
front with Car Nicholas, declared today
that every German soldier had been
driven from Russia south into the Gov
ernment of Suwalki.


The Car was within q dozen miles OF
his troops when by night attack they
captured the town of Bialla. (Blalla is
five miles inside the Prussian frontier
and 20 miles southwest OF Lyck.) The
Commander-in-C Chief afterward issued an
army order declaring the Cars visit will
inspire every one to new exploits such
as Russia never yet has seen.


The War Office has issued the following
statement:


THE Germans are now on the defensive.
They have all been driven back into East
Prussia, and by capturing Lyck and
Marggarbowa we have gained strategi-
cal position which puts the Germans in
a perilous situation


"On the left bank of the Vistula our
troops are now engaged with the Aus
trian and German armies Heavy fight
ing has been in progress for two days
without definite results. The enemy has
hurried heavy forces there to check our
advance on Slesia. We are making
gains"


This announcement has confirmed the
belief that the battle along the Vistula
north of Cracow has reached a critical
stage.


On the other hand, the Germans are
In force in Russian Poland having
reached almost to Warsaw. A German
official bulletin admits the Russians are
at Lyck.


Dispatches from Petrograd say that a
new Russian army has arrived at the
frontier near Posen, while another ia
marching toward Thorn.

Another German aerial raid upon Paris,

northeast and dropped bombs between
two crowded passengers trains that were
way station.


The missiles failed to explode, and were
later found imbedded in the earth two
feet beneath the surface.


Paris had not yet recovered from its
excitement over Sundays raid when the
second attack from the sky was sud-
denly and unexpectedly launched


Just short time before French aerial
patrols had returned after vainly securing
the sky for the two Taube machines that
had dropped eight bombs yesterday, KILL
ing four persons and wounding a.


The German attacks have failed to pro-
duCe the Panic that the Germans evil
IDENTIFY hoped for, but they have caused
a feeling of anxiety. 1t Is feared now
that night attack may be made and
that women and children will suffer
Among the French military authorities
and troops stationed here there Is feel
ing of stoicism out of keeping with the
excltable temperament of the French.


The aerial patrols have been warned
to exercise the most vigilant precautions,
and throughout the night the sky will
be swept with searchlghts every ten
minutes


Along with the eight bombs dropped by
the two daring Taubes on Sunday there
came into Paris n small German pennant,
bearing the following inscription:


"Wc have taken Antwerp; your turn
will come next


As showing the unbroken spirit of the
Parisians. some of the journalists face
tiousy referred to this pennant today as
"the Kaiser's calling card"

arc at the headquarters of General Gal
lieni. Military Governor of Paris.

hind the Cathedral; near the barracks OF

station: upon a coal depot near the sta

Marazlne Menagere in the Boulevard

LONDON, August %, 4:35 a.m.-The
Antwerp correspondent of the Morning
Post tells a vivid story of the adven-
lures of 500 men of the Belgian army at
Liege who arrived at Namur Saturday
afternoon after twenty days of lighting
and marching.


At the opening of the war their post
was between the Liege forts Chaudfon-
taine and Embourg Wednesday night of
the first week of the war orders were
given them to evacuate their position.
but the orders never reached this bat
talon, which became isolated by the Ger
mans. but with a strong fort on each
flank.


The Germans were aware of their pres
ence, but did not know their strength.
and the Belgians intrenching were able
to hold out eight days after the retire
ment of the main Belgian field force and
repulsed constant German attacks.


Finally, when their rations ran short
they succeeded in breaking through the
German lines, and after many hair
breadth escapes reached Seraing This
was not accomplished without several
brushes with the enemy, during which
many of their number were wounded.


They reached Huy Saturday, after the
railway authorities made up a train and
took them to Namur.

BIRMINGHAM, ALA, Feb. 20
Posses, with bloodhounds, to-day are
searching for bandits who held up
Queen and Crescent passenger train
No. 1 near Trussville, fourteen mics
north of here, late last night, and es-
capped with loot reported to be worth
$4,000.


In a battle with FIVE railway mes-
sengers, the robbers stabbed Harry
T. Melville, chief messenger; subdued
his companions and disappeared in
the darkness with the registered mail
sacks.


The train was bound from New
York to New Orleans and carried a
heavy passenger list.


~ Masked Men Beard Train.


After the train had passed Alfalfa,
56 miles north of here, and the last
scheduled stop before reaching Bir-
mingham. it was tagged. and when
the engineer reduced the speed of his
locomotive three masked men leaped
into the cab Covering the engineer
and fireman with pistols. the bandits
ordered the train stopped in lonely,
densely wooded spot between Truss
Vile and Irondale.


At that point the robbers COM
manded the train crew 10 .uncouple
the mail and express cars from the
rest of the train. After carrying these
cars about a mile, the locomotive was
again stopped and the mail cars were
detached.


Chief Messenger Melville. knowing
that the unusual actions of the train
meant holdup, barricaded his door
and told his assistants to prepare for
a fight. The original three bandits
were reinforced, and all were heavily
armed. When Melville refused to
open the door of his car. the bandits
began firing at it.


Slabs Chief Messenger.


Volley after volley was fired. and
the door was splintered. Finally the
bandits forced an entrance. but Me-
vile still showed fight When he
attempted to prevent the leader Of the
gang from taking possession of the
registered mail, the robber drew a
long knife and plunged 1t into the
messengers shoulder.


In the meantime, the other messen
gers, cowed by the display of firearms,
were standing with their hands above
their heads.


The cars were ransacked, the rob-
bers taking their time for their work.
However, they overlooked one sack
that contained mail worth $4,000.


Melville, after the robbery, said
that he believed there were about
eight men in the party, VINO
swarmed into the mail cars while
others were on guard at t.-e locomo-
tive.


William Murphy. engineer Of the
train, said that he was behind time
when the first signal was flashed near
Alfalfa. Believing that there was dan
ger ahead, he Immediately slowed
down. The men who entered the cab,
Murphy said, were armed with rifles.
The passengers thought that the train
had been delayed by an accident.


AS soon as word of the holdup was
received here a special train was
made up and rushed to the scene.
Deputy sheriffs Of Jefferson County
accompanied the railroad detectives.
taking several bloodhounds with
them.

New York, Sept. 5.-The closeness OF
the National League race means that the
magnates who faced huge losses about
July /, either will make money this year
or do no worse than break even. The
Braves along about Independence Day
looked sure to lose about $4,000 during
the season. Their marvellous spurt has
made them the greatest drawing card In
the game, and even II they don't win the
pennant they ought to finish the season
something like $4,000 to the good.


The Cardinals. playing the best and
most consistent game OF baseball that
has been exhibited by any st. Louis team
for years, will make money this year.
They have drawn big crowds at home
and big crowds abroad. Even the Cubs.
who got away to a miserable start, both
financially and in team standing. will
finish the season with a profit unless they
should go to pieces suddenly.


Giants Are Ahead.


The Giants, Of course, will finish with q
big profit. They have drawn compare
lively large crowds all year on the road
and the crowds at their home games,
especially with some close rival as the
opposing team, have nearly always pack
ed the immense Brush stadium


The Pirates. Dodgers, and Phillies will
not make money, but they aren't going
to lose very much. Most likely they will
break even. A month ago they looked
like big losers. but the fact that four
teams are punched for the vhirl into the
home stretch means that each will draw
crowds to the parks, no matter where
they are playing.


During the series in the West the Cubs
and Cardinals drew big crowds, even
when the Dodgers and Phillies constitut-
ed the enemy. and the share Of the re-
ceIpts that the visiting teams got for the
series ran far into FIVE figures


The Pirates are not drawing well at
home. except when the Braves and
Giants are the attraction, but they ought
to make up any deficit on their last swing
around the East when they battle with
the Giants and Bostonese in these cities.


The Reds, for the first time in many
years. may break ahead Of the game.
They made money Up to July last because
they were in the fight almost up to that
time. For the next six weeks they lost.
but the games with the Braves and
Giants in Cincinnati helped to swell the
income figures. Another windfan awaits
them when they make their last tour Of
the East.


American Is Different.


The situation is different in the Amer
lean League. Outside OF the Athletics
only one or two clubs will make money,
and even their Profits will be small The
Athletics will be lucky clearing $1,000
this season despite the great showing
they have made.


Almost a month ago II looked certain
that the Athletics would win the pennant.
They overshadowed every other team in
the league. and few fans went out to
the games in which they participated.
They wanted TO see a contest and with
the Athletics on one side Il lost the sem
blance Of a conteEt-just became a slaugh-
ter.


With the Athletics holding such a COM
manding lead the fans in other cities
felt the home team had no chance for
the honors. And when the fans feel that
way the turnstiles don't whiz like they
do in the days when the home team has a
fighting chance for the bunting.

In the West, the Golden Belt route,
which extends from Kansas City through
Topeka, Abilne. and Oakley to Denver.
has been put in excellent condition, and
as the shortest route between Kansas

The most important single improvement

trouble than heretofore and without the

road avoids such grades as exist on

The free September wind blew Ede's
full blue skirt about her as she stood
reading the letter which she had just
taken from the wayside box. From the
first sentence her face had gathered
trouble and perplexity. She made an
impatient movement as she turned the
page and read the last paragraph;


I'VE want to come. Mildred, Louise and
l. Being so near. We feel we cannot go
away without seeing you. OF course. we
can only stay the one day, but so much
may be said in one day, We can motor
out quite early and go back by moon
light"


EIDE drew a deep breath. Lifting her
eyes, she looked before her at the un-
kempt yard, the old weathered house
which was growing decrepit in places, at
the litter about the barns, and her heart
sank She was seeing it as they would
see it when they came. And they must
come. She could not deny them


Yes, they must come" she said aloud.
She put the letter back into the en-
velope and turned slowly toward tue
house.


Her impulse was to steal away INTO
some secret corner of the old house ana
cry her eyes out. but tears TOOK Tune
and she needed every moment She must
work-work in haste, for at the latest
the women would be there in three days.


During those three days EIDE fought
dirt, disorder and herself with all the
vim the occasion aroused. She made the
old house as inviting possible, but even
desperate ingenuity could not conceal the
holes in curtains and carpets, broken wall
paper and worn paint. When 1t came TO
the actual question OF food she could 90
better. She had cream and eggs and late
garden truck and chickens 10 conJure
with. The grapes were ripening on the
lattered treiiis and for decoration she
could go to the asters and golden-rod. She
could feed her guests well. AS for table,
ware, her wedding silver and linen had
been carefully kept. She sighed often
as she rubbed and polished. remembering
her wedding day and the events that had
gone before it.


There had been four of them in New
York-I.ouise Creston, Mildred Blair,
katherine Crosby and herself. Louise
wrote. Mildred painted, Katherine paint
cd and she taught They had been very
valiant, very full of enthusiasm and am
bition. But success tarried There was
together. Mildred's pictures would not
sell. neither would Louise's stories:
Katherine had few pupils. and she her
self had taught almost at a starvation





determinedly. Then she fell ill of a cold
contracted by tramping sodden pave
ments in thin shoes. When spring came
1t was evident she must go to the country
to recuperate. She had just money
enough to keep her for one season on
farm. 1t was a poor place. but she got
sunshine and air and clean water to
drink.


One day when she was tramping home
from the village where she had gone to
get some note paper a farmer overlook
her. He pulled up his horses and asked
her to ride. She was very tired, for the
road was dusty and long. She climbed
into the wagon beside the farmer. She
was too tired and dazed just at first to
see that he was young. Afterward she
came to like his face. They got ac-
quainted during the ride. So it began.
Before the summer ended she was en-
gagged to him.


She loved him. and the prospect Of the
future lived with him in the old house

bowmen, according to Jomini. the mill
tary historian, acquitted themselves
creditably against the French, who were
equipped with the latest firearms. 1t

arrow on Il European battlefield.

SAN FRANCISCO. Jan. 27.-Santa
Fe train No. 10, the Chicago mail, is
lost somewhere in the flood-stricken
San Gabriel valley, near Santa Bar
bara, according to advices received
here today by railroad officials.


The mail train, carrying more than
100 passengers, was last reported near
Monrovia, in the center of the flood
district. Then the wires went down.
and repeated efforts to learn whether
the passengers are in danger failed
early today.


Though but four persons are known
to have perished in the flood area, late
reports today indicate this number will
be increased by at least five. Condi-
tions near Santa Barbara and in the
Sacramento and San Joaquin Valleys
were reported improving today, but at
Bakersfield, the Kern river still Is ris-
ing, rain still is falling, and the situa-
ton is growing more critical hourly.


With four known to be dead and
railway traffic completely paralyzed, no
cessation of the unprecedented rainfall
which has inundated the entire Pacific
coast was in sight today. Taroughout
California streams are far cit of their
banks, cities are flooded, and miles Of
railroad tracks have been washed out.


The known dead, according to reports
received today, are:


RICE RODRIGUEZ, laborer, drowned
near Whittier.


HUGHES HAVEN, drowned near
Monrovia-


LOUIS JONES, banker, and his wife,
drowned at Montecito. near Santa Bar
bara. A lad was reported to have fallen
into the Los Angeles river at Los
Angeles.


The greatest damage has been done
at Santa Barbara 1t is known that
hundreds of houses were flooded.


Throughout California overland trains
are marooned. Telegraph and telephone
service is badly crippled in California,
and the Northwest. Portland, Seattle,
and other north coast cities report a
terrific forty-eight hour gale.

hear their spirits singing

The Philadelphia Orchestra gave the
second of their seasons concerts in WASH
ington yesterday afternoon at the New
National Theater. Miss Florence Hinkle.
soprano. was the soioist.


The program was devoted wholly to
Wagner. Opening with the Lohengrin
Vorspiel. the orchestral numbers were:
The Tannhauser Overture and venusberg

Farewell the Fire Music from THE
Walkure," the "Waldweben" from Sieg-
fried, and the Funeral March," 'Sieg-
fried's Death" and the finale from the
"Gotterdammerung"


In the Vorspiel from Lohengrin the
diminuendo after the climax and the
close were artistically very fine, but the
orchestra did not begin with the degree
OF pianissimo to give dynamic room for
the long and gradual working to the cli-
max. nor for the due expression of the
mysterious, ethereal atmosphere which
pervades the beginning Of that work.
With the exception OF this single criti-
cism the afternoons performance through
out was I'm the highest degree mastery.


The Tannhauser overture was superbly
played. Especially was the motive of
temptation and struggle worked up to a
ttHlcuuOuS anu tndknLCtnt the
motive of exaltation and remuneration.
with occurrences of the struggle motive
in the background, was also exquisite
work. So, again, in the Walkure music
the weaving OF the wotan strands with
the threads of the Fire Music. each full
of mythic suggestion, was rendered with
great power. But most beautiful of all.
richest in lustrous Oriental coloring. pic
torially perfect. was the playing of the
marvellous "Waldweben" scene from
Siegfried. The Funeral March was
given a deeply tragic rendering. The
finale of the ''Gotterdammerung"- stu
rendered with clarity and justice to the
significance OF each thematic thread.


Miss Hinkle has a soprano voice OF
great purity and sweetness. and capable
of an unusual range of emotional and
dramatic expression. "Elsa's Traum,''

with some constraint, but in the two arias
from Tannhauser-"EliZabet Gebet"

force. The audience was delighted and
manifested its pleasure in renewed sp-
plause.


Miss Hinkle was originally from Phila-
deiphia. but is now living in. New York.
She studied first with Oscar Saenger. and
later with witherspoon. She has an ex-
perience of six years of song recital work
to her credit, and judging from her work
of yesterday has a promising career be-
fore her.

Correspondence Of the Associated Press


OSTEND, Belgium, November 21-
The normal life of this usually lively
city has been radically changed by the
German military occupation. Inhabit-
ants are forbidden to leave their houses
between In the evening and in the
morning, and no lights may be shown
during that time. No one can leave
town without passports from the Ger
man authorities.


The usual market gatherings are al
most suspended. Villagers from out
side Ostend can come in only when at
tended by their burgomaster. and the
market hours are limited to Monday
and Thursday mornings.


Food Carried in Dog Carts.


All horses have been taken by the
military authorities. so only dog carts
can be used to bring food into the
town. Butter, eggs. meat and vegeta-
bles are cheap. but Ostend is without
fish. because all fishermen have fled to
England. Fishing would be impossible
because civilians are forbidden to ap-
proach the coast and the inhabitants Of
houses along the seashore have been
expelled.


The railways and electric trans have
been stopped for everything except mil
itary purposes and are being used night
and day for sending provisions to the
front and bringing back wounded.


Little is left of what formerly was
Westende, Dixmude, Schoore, Rams
kapellem. st. Picters. Capelle and Men
nekensvere, and over $50 farms in the
neighborhood have been destroyed.


Hundreds of wounded Belgfans and
French are brought to Ostend. and
those who can stand the journey are
sent along to Germany. A dozen or
more Germans. dead from their wounds,
are buried here every day. The wound
ed allies are we'll cared for by the Ger
mans.


Germans Make Heavy Requisitions.


Ostend IL without newspapers. soap.
oil, candles and coffee. The Germans
have made heavy acquisitions not only
Of foodstuffs in large quantities. but of
cigars and wine and all available mat
tresses and covers as well as clothing,
linen. wire and bicycles. For the prop
erty taken the Germans have given
reQuisition notes amounting to $1.000,-
900. The hotels are occupied by Ger
man officers. who live on the best of
everything. German bands play in the
parks every day. but have only the
Germans as auditors, because the In
habitants who are left boycott them.

POUGHkEEPSIE, n. T., January 23-
Elizabeth Fisher, twelve years old,
plunged through hole in the ice in Fish
Kill creek yesterday, clutched her six
year-old brother in one hand. and while
the swift current carried them under
she thumped with her other hand upon
the solid ice above them. Through re-
narkable herosm she saved the life of
the child. She is threatened with pneu-
monia, but is happy.


When Malcolm plunged into the water
Elizabeth did not hesitate a second. She
did not stop to remove her coat or her
shoes but leaped into the water just
as she saw the current carry her little
brother under the ice.


A dozen feet under the ice she caught
him. The swift current carried them on
down stream. and twenty or thirty feet
away was the next bend. The ice there
was broken and Elizabeth brought her
brother to the surface. The current
threw them against the bank and the
girl struggled out. drawing her brother
with her.


No one was in sight and Elizabeth
started back across the fields toward her
home, carrying her brother. When she
reached home she was almost exhausted.

From the Chicago Journal.


The corn clubs of the last few years
have proved that the corn belt of the
Mississippi valley extends much farther
south than had been supposed. This
means that the fertile corn, pork and
stock area tributary to Chicago markets
is greater than any one dreamed a
decade ago; nor is this demonstration
the only service rendered by this
rivalry of boys to see which can raise
the best acre of corn for the least
money.


These lads of the corn clubs have
nroyed that the soil of the United States
is seldom more than scratched. One
Kentucky boy produced a yield five
times as great as that which his father
secured from exactly similar land all
around The cost of cultivation per
acre was higher for the boys crop
than for the fathers. but the son had
a lower cost per bushel than his sire


Instances like these help to bring
home the truth that the soil throughout
most of the United States is richer
than ,hat on which Europe raises far
larger crops and supports vastly
denser population. Except for the val
lev Of the Pc and the delta of the
Rhine there is no part of Europe which
has such depth of soil and such fer
tiIity as prevails throughout most of the
Mississippi valley.

DENVER, Jan. 17.--"Mother" Jones,
who has been in the Trinidad mine
district here for sometime. is gen
tie soul despite her militant doc
trine.


She is past eighty, and her hair
is white.


And from her shrewd gray eyes
there flashes still glance that re-
veals soul that is young and full
Of optimism.


Those eyes belong to the woman
whom thousands of American miners
call Mother


Mother" Jones nursed the injured
in the great Chicago fire. Then she
went to the cotton mills of the South
and fought against the evils of child
labor. Ten years ago she went into
West Virginia, during the first an
thracite strike. called out 10000 mine
workers, the boys" and left an or
ganization of 10000 free miners"


One day a white faced messenger
burst into the Governors office with
the startling information that the "old
woman was marching upon the
State House with 1900 miners. Gov
ernor Glasscock met them upon the
Capitol steps and heard their dec
laration Of war.


They gave him twenty four hours
to get rid of the mine guards. Then
Mother" Jones travelled up and down
the Great Kanawha, and sent the
miners with their guns to the aid of
Paint Creek.


Suffered Terrible Hardships.


Yet, despite her untiring energy,
her ability to put up with terrible
hardships, Mary Harris Jones has
never lost those qualities that cause
her to be called Mother"


Reaching a town one morning dur
ing her work in West Virginia, prac-
tically dominated by the influence of
rich young mine owner, Mother"
Jones applied for permission to the
authorities to hold mass meeting.


She was refused the permit unless
she could gain the consent of the
mine owner himself


She sought the mine owner in his
home. She told him that she had
come to make a request which she
saw in his face he would grant.


He smiled and asked who she was
and what she desired With the
benignity of the most gentle kind
illness and simple dignity the old lady
replied demurely that she was Moth
er" Jones, and wished to have a talk
with his employees.


Meets Mine Owner.


You Mother Jones'" said the
rich man. astonished, you are sure
iy not in earnest?'


The mine owner studied the face,
the attitude, the folded hands of the
woman before him, and then inquired
what she would like to have him do.


Mother" Jones said she would lii,
to have him send word through Il s
mines that she was there, and grant
her permission to talk on Sunday in
an open space near the plymouth on
his own property.


Her rough meeting with things as
they are has not destroyed her hope
or dimmed the edge of her optimism.


How we have progressed" she
cries. Both labor and capital are
becoming imbued with the idea that
it is better to get together and talk
things out.

PANAMA. April %, 1914


Rock and dirt are still moving down
the Cucaracha slide into the Culebra cut,
but the engineers who have been fight
ing the treacherous slides in this vicin-
ity. are at last gaining upon nature
Fears that the opening of the canal set
for January, 1915. would have to be post
poned indefinitely, have been growing
less each day. for the dredges and steam
shovels have been taking out the dirt
and rock much faster than it slid into
the canal.


The Culebra slide, just to the south of
the Cucaracha trouble, is entirely at rest
and it is hoped it will remain SO, but the
canal engineers will watch this treacher-
hillside with some anxiety as the
any season approaches. Breaks already
are showing far back from the canal
prism, and these may indicate move
ment which might any day precipitate
tons of crushed rock and dirt into the
canal for the tireless dredges and steam
shoyels to remove. The coming wet sea-
son will be likely to loosen anything
ready to slide.

PRESIDIO. Texas. January 3.-Twc
thousand Mexican refugees. including
half-staryed women and children and
some federal deserters. rushed across the
river to the United States today to seek
protection from the battle at Ojinaga,
Mexico. opposite here.


Savage fighting between rebels and fed
erals at Ojinaga continued throughout
the night and was still in progress this
morning.


The besieged federals, who were thrown
into a panic at the first onslaught of
the rebels, today were resisting stubborn
ly all attempts OF the attacking army to
drive them from the town.


Report Heavy Federal Losses.


Before daybreak the artillery fire of
the rebels, which had continued all night
before, became more furious. A rain of
shells descended on the federal intrench-
ments. Wounded soldiers who found
their way across the river told the Amer
lean Red Cross officials that the federal
losses were heavy.


During the night about 200 federals
made a desperate sortie and from the
river bottom about half mile from
Ojinaga, attempted to dislodge the rebels.
But the constitutionalists opened fire on
them with machine guns and whipped
them back. with severe losses.


Bullets on American Side.


Scattering bullets fell on the Ameri-
can side today. but no American was
injured. Fresh Red Cross supplies which
had been urgently needed arrived today.
Nurses and physicians are preparing to
care for the large number of wounded
they expect TO find on the field at the
conclusion of the battle.

today. A report that the money had been
stolen proved untrue. The money was
rushed across the river in the hope Of
encouraging the federal soldiers Gems.

sent word that they had no intention OF
abandoning the town. The rebels have
been reinforced until they numbered to-
day $500 A fresh supply of ammunition

here, had reached a point about 100
yards beyond the. station.

arrival of the mail. hurried to the
place where the pouches were thrown
off and found that two pouches were
missing. He declares, however, that


he saw nobody near the pouches.
No Clue to Theft.


AS the hour was very early and the
light was extremely poor, the thief
may have seized the pouches and es-
capped without being seen.
The theft was reported to the Post


Office Department and to the offices of
the railroad, and post office inspectors
and railway detectives have been
working on the case. So far, however.
not the slightest clue has been discov-
cred that might lead to the apprehen-
sion of the thief.


Yesterdays theft was the fifth that
has occurred since the early morning
of September l. In none Of these cases

rings out the old year." Despite the inevita-

bed of the old year, the new is welcomed
with warm greetings and hearty anticipa-
tions.

Romans as man with two faces, one look
ing backward, the other forward. implying
that he stood between the old and the new
year with a regard to both. 1t is the for
ward look that characterizes popular new
year celebrations. Men meet each other with
greetings of good will. There is an unusual
social freedom which, on occasion, may break
down the barriers of conventional conduct

tacular obserVances.

Paris. June 6.--French naval authori-
ties attach great Importance to Admiral
Percy Scotts opinion that submarines
and aircraft render Dreadnoughts obso-
lete This is not a new theory in
France, for Admiral Aube, the French
Minister Of Marine. as long ago as 1885
contendel that torpedo boats made bat
tleships useless. putting his theory into
practice. France ceased building battle
ships. putting all her naval construction
funds into swift cruisers and torpedo
boat destroyers. Naval experts soon dis
covered that fatal error had been COM
mitted, and building plans were re-
yersed, giving prominence to battleships.


The board OF experts is coming 10 the
conclusion that capital ships are abso-
lutely necessary. Naval supremacy
rests With ocean keeping ships, while
torpedo boats and submarines are simply
weapons for coast defence. with limited
offensive powers The naval authorities
and the Minister of Marine to-day do
not indorse the views OF Sir Percy Scott.
but pin their faith on seasoine ships
with big long range runs.


II is significant that Jean Jaures, the
Unified Socialist leader. and the anti
military political parties have already
adopted Sir Percy Scott's theory as a text
for urging the reduction Of French naval
expenditure.

with Georgetown clearly set forth.

the athletic association from fulfilling
existing contracts. Three base ball
contests have been scheduled for this
spring.

HAMPTON ROADS, Va. July 1s.-
Having covered more than 1000 miles on

VENICE, via Paris, September 25.-
A graphic picture of conditions of life
in Vienna is revealed in an official
statement of the mayor of Vienna that
his city is supporting the families of
$4,000 reservists at daily cost Of $780,
900 and in addition is endeavoring to
provide for 100000 unemployed and
another 100000 fugitives from Galicia
and the crownland Of Bukowina.


For the fugitives Of the city already
has expended $1,000,000.


10000 Are Helpless.


According to the mayors statement
100000 unemployed have been given po-
sitions on the public works, but the
remaining $4,000 are helpless. The
mayor complains that there has been
an inadequate response to his appeals
for the various war relief funds and
says many wealthy persons have with
held subscriptions upon the plea that
they did not know which fund to
assist


The first official report of the Aus
trian Red Cross shows that the total
contributions to it's fund amounted to
only $4,000. The report says that
the rich industrial classes, for the most
part, subscribed literally, but ex-
presses disappointment at the small
contributions of many enormously
wealthy aristocratic land owners.


Generosity Among Poor.


The middle and even the lower class
es, the report adds, have shown them
selves more generous.


Polish newspapers say that when
OCCUPYING Lemberg the Russians
showed the utmost consideration for
the population. They paid cash for
all supplies taken,- placed sentries to
guard the public buildings and left
only enough troops behind to main
tain order. Nearly half the popula-
tion fled the city, but the remainder
are living in perfect quiet and Sc
curity, according to the newspapers.

gagged and that the French are re-
gaining ground here ceded in the

pared to aid the allies in keeping

coast bases.

movement in Galicia was for the

entrenched positions along the
Donajec River and was not a re-
treat as the Austrians claim.

fee statement says that material
progress is being made against

city is considered certain. The
general situation in France con-
tinues unchanged with the Germans
making steady gains on the right
wing.

the German fire from the Kiaochow
forts slackening and it is believed

AWHILE, Pa, Sept. A.-Battered
and bruised but happy, the members of
the Lebanon Valley College football
team returned to school today after their
successful stand against the Carlisle
Indians yesterday. Coach Guyer gave
the team days vacation today. To-
morrow the team starts its regular rou-
tine work for the game next Saturday
when they meet the Carlisle Indian Re.
serves.


Although defeated yesterday, the play
ers consider their showing a virtual
victory over the Indians. They out
played Coach Warmers team and forced
the playing during most of the time
Twice they forced the Indians to their
two-yard line. but each time the Off
cials caught the runner out of bounds
and the Indians were given the ball
The showing made yesterday Is better
than ever before in the schools history
and hopes are being entertained for
championship team this season.


Last night huge bonfires were built on
the campus and the students, male and
coed, danced around the flames, singing
their songs of victory. When considered
the short time that the local collegians
have been practicising their showing in
yesterdays game was almost wonderful.
Coach Warner congratulated Coach Guyer
on the excellent showing of his team
and declared that their work was equal
to any seen on the Carlisle field in years.

DENVER, Jan. 17-"Mother" Jones,
who has been in the Trinidad mine
district here for sometime, is a gem
tie soul, despite her militant doc
trine


She is past eighty, and her hair
is white.


And from her shrewd gray eyes
there flashes still a glance that re-
veals soul that is young and full
of optimism.


Those eyes belong to the woman
whom thousands of American miners
call Mother"


Mother" Jones nursed the injured
in the great Chicago fire. Then she
went to the cotton mills of the South
and fought against the evils of child
labor Ten years ago she went into
West Virginia, during the first an
thraCite strike, called out 10000 mine
workers, "the boys" and left an or
ganization of 10000 free miners"


One day d white-faced messenger
burst INTO the Governors Office with
the startling information that the "old
woman was marching upon the





ernor Glasscock met them upon the
Capitol steps and heard their dec
laratiOn of war


They gave him twenty four hours
to get rid of the mine guards. Then
Mother" Jones travelled up and down
the Great kanawha, and sent the
miners with their guns to the aid of
Paint Creek.


Suffered Terrible Hardships.


Yet, despite her untiring energy,
her ability to put up with terrible
hardships, Mary Harris Jones has
never lost those qualities that, cause
her to be called Mother"


Reaching a town one morning dur
ing her work in West Virginia, prac-
tically dominated by the influence of
a rich young mine owner, Mother
Jones applied for permission to the
authorities to hold a mass meeting.


She was refused the permit unless
she could gain the consent of the
mine owner himself


She sought the mine owner in his
home. She told him that she had
come to make a request which she
saw in his face he would grant.


He smiled and asked who she was
and what she desired. With the
benignity of the most gentle kind
liness and simple dignity the old lady
replied demurely that she was Moth
err Jones, and wished to have a talk
with his employees.


Meets Mine Owner.


You Mother Jones'" said the
rich man, astonished, you are sure
ly not in earnest?"


The mine owner studied the face,
the attitude, the folded hands of the
woman before him, and then inquired
what she would like to have him do.


Mother Jones said she would like
to have him send word through his
mines that she was there, and grant
her permission to talk on Sunday in
an open space near the plymouth on
his own property.


Her rough meeting with things as
they are has not destroyed her hope
or dimmed the edge of her optimism.


How we have progressed" she
cries. Both labor and capital are
becoming imbued with the idea that
it is better to get together and talk
things out

Heavy gales in the early part of last
week gave the vessels of the revenue cut
ter service on the stations between Cape
Hatteras and Cape Cod, plenty to do in


aiding vessels in distress and in saving


lives and property endangered in winter
storms. The cutters 1tasca, Gresham and
Acushnet on the Nantucket shoals and
Vineyard sound stations and the cutter
Apache the Chesapeake station have


been called upon to do the bulk OF the


relief work and reports received at the


headquarters of the service in the Treas


ury show that eighteen vessels have been


aided by the cutters named since Mon


day last.
Thursday last the Acushnet was in
touch at one time with ten vessels ask


Ing assistance and reports state that
eighteen schooners and one tug were in
sight of Chatham, Mass. at one time,
with flags flying with union down, asking
for aid. These vessels were all covered


with ice and this condition seems to have
been their chief trouble.


The men in the cutters shave worked in


icy cold gales in adm. vessels and it is
said that several members Of the cutter
crews have been frost bitten.


Braved Storm and Ice.
The cutters fought their way through
storm and ice to the vessels, and though
themselves covered with ice. which the


men have not had time to clean away,


they are going night and day to get into


harbor the vessels needing help. While


the cutters on the New England coast in
former years have been called upon to
aid many vessels in trouble, this is the
first time since the establishment of the


winter cruising service that practically
every vessel on Nantucket sound was in


need of help.


Since Monday last, among other vessels,
the cutter Acushnet has brought into
Vineyard Haven the schooners Silver
Spray. Daniel McLoud. Sunlight and she
then went to the aid of the schooner War
ner Moore and half dozen other craft
The cutter ltasca carried into Province


town, Mass, schooners John Hart I'd,
and Pearl Nelson and earlier in the week
she took the schooner Henry Miller into
Vineyard Haven. She also took the
schooner Luther r. GarIetson from Nam
tucket to Vineyard Haven. In trouble off
Monomoy point, the schooner Meservey
was picked up by the cutter Gresham and
taken to Prorincetown. The Gresham also
aided the four-masted schooner Mount
Hope, which was found at anchor off


Chatham leaking badly. by carrying her


into a safe harbor where repairs could be


made.

Pans, June 2i.-The letter carriers
strike was practically ended to-day by
tine action of .Gaston Thomson, Minister
OF Commerce Posts and Telegraphs. who
promised to make a thorough investiga-
ton OF the strikers grievances II they
would return to work. Fifteen minutes
after the deputation OF the letter car
riers to whom the promise was made left
the Minister'S office the postal service
was again In full operation and the men
were working furiously to handle the ac-
cumuiated mail and restore the service
to its usual basis.


Before the agreement was reached the
800 letter carriers who held possession
OF the central post office last night and
prevented the distribution OF the mails
we're still barricaded within the post Of
flee They quickly exhausted their small
supply OF food, but comrades managed
to run the blockading force OF 500 po-
licemen who surrounded the block and
brought fresh supplies, which were hauled
la through the windows.


The police were considering whether
to storm the building and drive the strik-
ers out when peace was restored by the
action OF the Minister. The latter was
waited upon this morning by u deputa-
tation OF business men who told him that
the city already had suffered loss OF
5000, 600 through the few hours delay and
that unless immediate steps were taken
to restore the service the loss would be
enormous


The strike was caused by the refusal
OF the Senate to incorporate in the postal
budget Increased allowances which the
letter carriers have been urging.

yards. The German statement,
speaking of this engagement, says
that the French attack was
partly repelled." French claims
to progress in Belgium are denied
in Berlin, where it is said that the
British have suffered reverses at

no developments in the east, say
ing merely that the fighting is
continuing. The. French state
ment, however, asserts that the
Russians are pressing forward

the East Prussian frontier, but
admits that the Germans have
made progress in the fighting in
Poland, to the west of Warsaw.

ton from Petrograd, in the same
breath, admits that the Russians
have been compelled to retreat
from some positions, and asserts
that the German attacks have
been repulsed everywhere with
heavy losses to the invaders.
Germany and Austria continue to
assert that important successes
are being achieved.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 5,-Members of the
Interstate Commerce Commission recon-
vened today in executive session, this
being the first meeting of the fall ses-
sion The conference today was largely
perfunctory, reviewing the work for the
winter session and exchanging Views on
the cases the individual commissioners
heard at various points throughout the
country during the summer.


During the week it is expected that the
commission will give some consideration
to the decisions which are to be issued
this fall in the so-called water line cases.
Under the Panama Canal act the rail-
roads are not permitted to continue their
ownership and operation of water lines
unless they have permission to do so
from the commission.


The commission will not Immediately
prosecute the proposed Investigations into
the Pere Marquette and other railroads
because of the unsettled financial situa-
tion.

our God, of war and peace,

half one can read.


Most authorities are inclined to give
Benjamin Franklin credit for the inven-
ton. He was. SO the story goes. an in
veterate reader and could not use his
reading glasses when looking any dis
lance away. Finally the notion came to
him that he could combine his glasses,
and he thereupon had the lenses cut in
half and one half of each lens placed
in the rim of each spectacle rim. The
result was that a single pair Of glasses
was sufficient, though present day ocu-
lists state that the sharply drawn line

Pennsylvania will go to Pedro Miguel

the same time.

ces where parcel post and similar mat

railway mail cars from congestion and
for the designation of certain offices

be tested under the guidance of experts
from the departments, with the view to
standardizing the work In post offices
generally


New efforts have also been made to
bring the postal savings system closer
to the people, with the object of encour-
aging habits of thrift and saving.


Already the postal savings of the coun-
try are approximately $40OOO,OOO. and

ings abroad, as well as from secret hid
